YesWiki Bazar form-import volumetric POST — CVE-2026-46670 blind SQLi extraction loop AIExploitation High
Hunts the byte-by-byte extraction loop used to exploit CVE-2026-46670 in YesWiki. The PoC drives one POST to /?BazaR&vue=formulaire per character of the hex-encoded value being exfiltrated from yeswiki_users, producing dozens-to-hundreds of POSTs to a single URI from a single source IP in a short window — an unusual pattern for a wiki application. Rationale: Locks on the article's exact request shape (POST + csUriQuery containing both 'BazaR' and 'vue=formulaire') and the unavoidable property of the PoC: blind extraction requires N requests for N characters of the password hash, so a per-source-IP POST count >=20 in 5 min to this single endpoint is a strong signal that something other than a human is wiki-ing. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jwvv-qr7q-cv8j • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/blob/1f485c049db030b94c047ec219e63534ac81142e/tools/bazar/services/FormManager.php#L258
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate site admin bulk-importing many Bazar forms via the UI (will share a browser UA and a single authenticated session)
  • Synthetic monitoring / uptime probe configured to POST to the form endpoint
  • Internal QA / pentest team rerunning known-exploitation tests against staging
  • Migration script run by the site owner during a YesWiki version bump
  • Search-engine / crawler misbehavior submitting forms it shouldn't (rare, but cIP will resolve to crawler ASN)
Suppression filter
| where csUserName == ""  // exclude authenticated admin bulk-imports
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending cIP's full request stream for the window — confirm whether the POSTs come with the wiki's auth cookies set (legit admin import) or are bare (exploitation). Check scStatus distribution; an exploitation loop typically returns 200/302 consistently. 2) Contain: block the source IP at WAF/edge and snapshot the YesWiki DB. Force-rotate every account in yeswiki_users (assume the password column has been exfiltrated). Patch to >= 4.6.4 immediately. 3) Hunt: search yeswiki_nature for rows where bn_id_nature is in the 7000000-9999999 range (the PoC's arithmetic offset signature), grep yeswiki_users for sessions logged in after the exploitation window, and pivot the source IP across other internet-facing apps for parallel scanning.
let WindowMinutes = 5m;
let PostThreshold = 20;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod =~ "POST"
| where csUriQuery has "BazaR" and csUriQuery has "vue=formulaire"
| summarize Posts = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), UserAgents = make_set(csUserAgent, 5), Statuses = make_set(scStatus, 5), Stems = make_set(csUriStem, 3)
          by cIP, sSiteName, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMinutes)
| where Posts >= PostThreshold
| order by LastSeen desc

Non-browser User-Agent against YesWiki Bazar form-import endpoint — CVE-2026-46670 exploit tooling AIExploitation High
Hunts the PoC's exploit fingerprint: a request to /?BazaR&vue=formulaire from a scripting-language User-Agent (the published PoC uses Python-urllib/3.13). Real users post Bazar forms from a browser; a curl/python/PowerShell UA on this exact endpoint is high-signal for CVE-2026-46670 exploitation or reconnaissance. Rationale: The published PoC literally ships with User-Agent: Python-urllib/3.13 (from the Burp capture in the article body). The Bazar form-import endpoint is a low-traffic admin path on YesWiki; a scripting-language UA hitting it via POST is rarely benign and matches both the public PoC and copycat exploitation. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory at github.com/advisories/GHSA-jwvv-qr7q-cv8j. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jwvv-qr7q-cv8j
ATT&CKT1190 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate API-driven import tooling the site owner wrote (will originate from the wiki's own admin IP range)
  • curl/wget-based uptime monitoring that mistakenly probes the form-import endpoint
  • Yeswiki-admin CLI scripts that POST forms during migrations
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus / Burp) running an authenticated assessment
  • DevOps CI job seeding test forms after a deploy
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8","192.168.0.0/16","172.16.0.0/12")  // suppress internal admin/CI tooling; tune to your wiki's known-admin egress
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the source IP's recent activity — is it scanning broadly across other endpoints (mass scanner) or laser-focused on /?BazaR&vue=formulaire (targeted exploitation)? Check scStatus: 200 with growing csBytes return on each POST suggests blind data exfiltration is succeeding. 2) Contain: block the source IP at WAF/edge, then verify YesWiki version. If < 4.6.4, take the site offline pending patch and snapshot the DB. Treat yeswiki_users.password as exposed and force a global password reset. 3) Hunt: look back 30 days for any other source IPs hitting the same URI with non-browser UAs (the PoC is now public; expect copycats), and sweep all internet-facing YesWiki deployments in the estate for version <= 4.6.3.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod =~ "POST"
| where csUriQuery has "BazaR" and csUriQuery has "vue=formulaire"
| where csUserAgent has_any ("Python-urllib","python-requests","curl/","Go-http-client","Java/","PowerShell","wget","libwww-perl")
| summarize Hits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Statuses = make_set(scStatus, 5) by cIP, sSiteName, csUserAgent, csUriStem
| order by LastSeen desc

MiniUpdate UpdateChecker.dll sideload via legitimate signed .NET host AIInstallation High
Detects loading of the Screening Serpens MiniUpdate payload (internal name UpdateChecker.dll) by a legitimate signed .NET host process via DLL sideloading. The DLL is dropped alongside a hijack-vulnerable benign binary from the Hiring Portal.zip lure and loaded from non-standard user-writable directories. Rationale: Pivots on Unit 42's named internal DLL `UpdateChecker.dll` plus the eight published SHA256 hashes for the MiniUpdate RAT family. User-writable path filter mirrors Screening Serpens' Hiring Portal.zip ZIP-extract sideload chain. Cross-checked against Check Point's 2025 UNC1549 report and MITRE T1574.014 (AppDomainManager Injection). Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1019/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/iranian-cyber-actors-target-europe/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/014/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1574.014
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vendor auto-update DLLs coincidentally named UpdateChecker.dll (e.g. Logitech, third-party LOB apps) writing to %ProgramData%
  • Internal developer build artifacts where a DLL is named UpdateChecker.dll in a project workspace under \Users\<dev>\source\
  • Endpoint security agent update DLLs unpacked to a user temp directory
  • Chocolatey / Squirrel-based app installers staging update DLLs in AppData\Local
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !in~ ("Microsoft Corporation","Logitech","Adobe Systems Incorporated","VMware, Inc.") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the loading process from DeviceImageLoadEvents/InitiatingProcessFileName — confirm whether it is a legitimate signed .NET binary residing in a user-writable path alongside an unsigned UpdateChecker.dll and a .config file (AppDomainManager hijack pattern). Verify SHA256 against the published Unit 42 IOC list and VirusTotal. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the device in Defender/MDE, kill the host process, quarantine UpdateChecker.dll and the paired host EXE+config. Reset the user's AAD/M365 credentials and revoke active sessions — Screening Serpens targets technical staff for follow-on access. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the host process hash and command line across DeviceProcessEvents for the last 30 days. Search EmailEvents for Hiring Portal.zip / Senior Software Engineer*.pdf attachments and recruitment-themed lures to the affected user. Query DNS to the four published C2 domains.

Screening Serpens AppDomainManager hijack via .NET app .config tampering AIInstallation High
Detects writes of a .NET application configuration file (appname.exe.config) containing an `appDomainManagerAssembly` / `appDomainManagerType` entry that redirects CLR initialization to a sideloaded assembly. This is the core Screening Serpens 2026 evolution that disables target app security and loads MiniUpdate/MiniJunk V2 RATs. Rationale: Targets the specific Unit 42-described evolution: AppDomainManager hijacking that manipulates .NET initialization via a legitimate .config file. The pattern of a same-directory triple (legitimate signed EXE + attacker EXE.config + attacker DLL) in user-writable paths is highly specific to this campaign and rarely seen in legitimate software, which always installs to Program Files via MSI/trusted installers. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/014/ • https://pentestlab.blog/2020/05/20/persistence-appdomainmanager/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/iranian-cyber-actors-target-europe/
ATT&CKT1574.014 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer workstations where Visual Studio publishes a debug build to %USERPROFILE%\source\repos\<proj>\bin\ with associated app.config
  • Portable apps extracted to %APPDATA% that legitimately ship a .NET host + .config + DLLs (e.g. ShareX, Greenshot)
  • Internal LOB ClickOnce deployments dropping config+DLL pairs to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Apps
  • User-mode update agents staging new EXE+config bundles in %TEMP% before promoting them
Suppression filter
| where ConfigPath !startswith @"C:\Users\" or (ConfigPath !contains @"\source\repos\" and ConfigPath !contains @"\bin\Debug\" and ConfigPath !contains @"\bin\Release\" and ConfigPath !contains @"\AppData\Local\Apps\")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the written .exe.config file content for `<appDomainManagerAssembly>` and `<appDomainManagerType>` tags — legitimate app configs almost never set these. Verify the paired DLL is unsigned or signed by an unknown/suspicious publisher. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host in MDE. Quarantine the .config, the sideloaded DLL, and the legitimate host EXE (which would otherwise be re-triggered each launch). Disable the user's account and revoke tokens. Step 3 (hunt): Across the fleet, hunt for any other matching triples (signed .NET EXE + .config with appDomainManagerAssembly + unsigned DLL) in user-writable paths. Pull DNS for the four Screening Serpens C2 domains and any newly-created Azure-hosted *.cloudapp.azure.com / *.azurewebsites.net domains that received traffic from this host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".exe.config"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","wusa.exe","setup.exe","installer.exe","OfficeClickToRun.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName endswith ".dll"
    | where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\")
    | project DllTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DllFolder=FolderPath, DllName=FileName, DllSHA256=SHA256, DllWriter=InitiatingProcessFileName
) on DeviceId
| where abs(datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, DllTime)) < 300 and tolower(FolderPath) == tolower(DllFolder)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ConfigPath=FolderPath, ConfigName=FileName, DllName, DllSHA256, DllWriter, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let configWrites = ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".exe.config"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","wusa.exe","setup.exe","OfficeClickToRun.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ConfigPath=TargetFilePath, ConfigName=TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine;
let dllWrites = ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".dll"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project DllTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DllPath=TargetFilePath, DllName=TargetFileName, DllSHA256=TargetFileSHA256;
configWrites
| join kind=inner dllWrites on DvcHostname
| where abs(datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, DllTime)) < 300
| extend ConfigDir = substring(ConfigPath, 0, strlen(ConfigPath) - strlen(ConfigName))
| extend DllDir = substring(DllPath, 0, strlen(DllPath) - strlen(DllName))
| where tolower(ConfigDir) == tolower(DllDir)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ConfigPath, ConfigName, DllName, DllSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*.exe.config OR *.EXE.config OR *.exe.CONFIG)) (@TargetFilename:(*\\Users\\* OR *\\AppData\\* OR *\\Temp\\* OR *\\Downloads\\* OR *\\ProgramData\\*)) -@Image:(*\\msiexec.exe OR *\\MsiExec.exe OR *\\TrustedInstaller.exe OR *\\OfficeClickToRun.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\.exe\.config$/i
| TargetFileName=/\\(Users|AppData|Temp|Downloads|ProgramData)\\/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(msiexec|TrustedInstaller|OfficeClickToRun|GoogleUpdate|wusa|setup)\.exe$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\.dll$/i | TargetFileName=/\\(Users|AppData|Temp|Downloads|ProgramData)\\/i}, field=aid, key=DllAid, include=[TargetFileName, SHA256HashData, _time])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as process_name values(Filesystem.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.exe.config" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where match(file_path,"(?i)\\\\(Users|AppData|Temp|Downloads|ProgramData)\\\\") AND NOT match(process_name,"(?i)(msiexec|trustedinstaller|wusa|setup|installer|update)\.exe$")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as process_name values(Filesystem.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.exe.config" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where match(file_path,"(?i)\\\\(Users|AppData|Temp|Downloads|ProgramData)\\\\") AND NOT match(process_name,"(?i)(msiexec|trustedinstaller|wusa|setup|installer|update)\.exe$")
Screening Serpens C2 — DNS/network to UNC1549 infrastructure (Feb-Apr 2026) AICommand & Control High
Detects any DNS resolution or network connection to the four Unit 42-published Screening Serpens C2 domains used during the Feb-Apr 2026 espionage campaign against US, Israel, UAE and Middle Eastern targets. These domains are dedicated per-target/per-variant and seeing any single resolution is high-fidelity. Rationale: All four domains are explicitly named in the Unit 42 article as Screening Serpens C2 infrastructure for the Feb-Apr 2026 MiniUpdate/MiniJunk V2 campaign. The note `buisness-centeral-transportation.com` (deliberate typosquat of `business-central-transportation`) and `ramiltonsfinance.com` are highly unusual lures unlikely to appear in benign traffic. Cross-checked against MITRE G1019 (UNC1549) and Check Point's earlier Western Europe expansion report. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1019/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/iranian-cyber-actors-target-europe/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers / threat-intel analysts performing manual lookups of the published IOCs from analyst workstations
  • Sandbox / detonation systems resolving the domains during automated triage
  • Threat-intel platforms (MISP, OpenCTI, TIP) auto-enriching indicators with active DNS lookups
  • DNS sinkholing infrastructure that proactively resolves known-bad domains for telemetry
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","iexplore.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--headless","--no-sandbox","sandbox","cuckoo","anyrun")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the host and the InitiatingProcessFileName making the resolution/connection. If the process is a browser launched by an analyst, validate against ticket/case context. If it is a non-browser process (especially a .NET host with a sideloaded DLL), treat as confirmed Screening Serpens compromise. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host in MDE/Falcon. Block the four C2 domains at the secure web gateway and DNS firewall fleet-wide. Reset and force MFA re-enrollment for the user. Step 3 (hunt): Run the MiniUpdate sideload UC and AppDomainManager hijack UC against the same host. Search EmailEvents for Hiring Portal.zip and the six job-requisition PDFs (JR205894 pattern). Look for additional Azure-hosted (cloudapp.azure.com / azurewebsites.net) domains contacted by the same process — Unit 42 notes 3-5 unique Azure-hosted domains per target.
let c2Domains = dynamic(["business-startup.org","buisness-centeral-transportation.com","premierhealthadvisory.com","ramiltonsfinance.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (c2Domains) or RemoteUrl endswith ".business-startup.org" or RemoteUrl endswith ".buisness-centeral-transportation.com" or RemoteUrl endswith ".premierhealthadvisory.com" or RemoteUrl endswith ".ramiltonsfinance.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2Domains = dynamic(["business-startup.org","buisness-centeral-transportation.com","premierhealthadvisory.com","ramiltonsfinance.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where Name has_any (c2Domains)
| project TimeGenerated, Source="DnsEvents", Host=Computer, SrcIp=ClientIP, Query=Name, RemoteIp=tostring(IPAddresses)),
(ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (c2Domains)
| project TimeGenerated, Source="ImDnsActivity", Host=SrcHostname, SrcIp=SrcIpAddr, Query=DnsQuery, RemoteIp=tostring(DnsResponseName)),
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where DestinationHostName has_any (c2Domains) or DestinationDnsDomain has_any (c2Domains) or RequestURL has_any (c2Domains)
| project TimeGenerated, Source="CommonSecurityLog", Host=SourceHostName, SrcIp=SourceIP, Query=coalesce(DestinationHostName, DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL), RemoteIp=DestinationIP),
(ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where Url has_any (c2Domains) or HttpHostName has_any (c2Domains)
| project TimeGenerated, Source="ImWebSession", Host=SrcHostname, SrcIp=SrcIpAddr, Query=coalesce(HttpHostName, Url), RemoteIp=DstIpAddr)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

level: critical
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:windows.security OR source:zeek OR source:cisco-umbrella OR source:cloudflare) (@dns.question.name:(*business-startup.org OR *buisness-centeral-transportation.com OR *premierhealthadvisory.com OR *ramiltonsfinance.com) OR @network.destination.domain:(*business-startup.org OR *buisness-centeral-transportation.com OR *premierhealthadvisory.com OR *ramiltonsfinance.com) OR @http.url:(*business-startup.org* OR *buisness-centeral-transportation.com* OR *premierhealthadvisory.com* OR *ramiltonsfinance.com*) OR @QueryName:(*business-startup.org OR *buisness-centeral-transportation.com OR *premierhealthadvisory.com OR *ramiltonsfinance.com))

Screening Serpens recruitment lure — Hiring Portal.zip + job requisition PDFs AIDelivery High
Detects delivery of the Screening Serpens spear-phishing lure: an archive named Hiring Portal.zip (or nested within an outer ZIP) accompanied by job-requisition PDFs following the pattern '*Software Engineer*Job ID JR######*.pdf'. Targets technical personnel in aerospace, defense and telecom sectors. Rationale: Pivots on the specific lure filename `Hiring Portal.zip` named by Unit 42 (and previously by Check Point research as a Screening Serpens artifact), plus the documented job-requisition PDF pattern (e.g., `Senior Software Engineer Job ID JR205894.pdf`). Restricting to user-download locations cuts the FP rate from generic HR keyword matches on email gateways. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/iranian-cyber-actors-target-europe/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1019/
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate HR / recruitment workflow where corporate Workday/Greenhouse exports include 'Job ID JR######' in filenames for internal hiring managers
  • Job-seeker employees saving genuine recruiter outreach attachments named 'Hiring Portal' from real airlines/aerospace firms
  • Recruiting agencies sending bulk job-spec PDFs to engineering staff (sales pipeline noise)
  • Internal mobility programs auto-emailing job requisition PDFs from the ATS
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !in~ ("workday.com","greenhouse.io","lever.co","taleo.net","icims.com","smartrecruiters.com","linkedin.com") and SenderFromDomain !endswith "@<your-corp-domain>"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Examine the sender domain and infrastructure — confirm whether the email originates from a typosquat / lookalike domain impersonating a global air carrier or major aerospace firm (Unit 42 notes the March campaign impersonated a global air carrier). Detonate Hiring Portal.zip in a sandbox; look for the nested second Hiring Portal.zip and the six job-spec PDFs. Step 2 (contain): Soft-delete the email from all recipient mailboxes via Defender for Office 365. If the user already extracted the ZIP, isolate the device and quarantine the inner archive and any extracted EXE/DLL/.config triples. Step 3 (hunt): Pull DeviceImageLoadEvents for UpdateChecker.dll and DeviceFileEvents for *.exe.config writes on the recipient's host. Run the C2 domain hunt across the fleet. Search EmailEvents for the same sender across the org — Screening Serpens runs concurrent same-day campaigns against multiple targets in a region.
let lureFileNames = dynamic(["Hiring Portal.zip","Hiring_Portal.zip","HiringPortal.zip"]);
let email = EmailAttachmentInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where FileName in~ (lureFileNames) or FileName matches regex @"(?i)^.*Software Engineer.*Job ID JR\d{6}.*\.pdf$" or FileName matches regex @"(?i)^.*Senior.*Engineer.*Job ID JR\d{6}.*\.pdf$"
| join kind=leftouter (EmailEvents | project NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, FileName, FileType, SHA256, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation;
let host = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where (FileName in~ (lureFileNames)) or (FileName matches regex @"(?i)^.*(Software|Senior|Principal).*Engineer.*Job ID JR\d{6}.*\.pdf$")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Desktop\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl;
union email, host
| order by Timestamp desc
let lureFileNames = dynamic(["Hiring Portal.zip","Hiring_Portal.zip","HiringPortal.zip"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where TargetFileName in~ (lureFileNames) or TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^.*(Software|Senior|Principal).*Engineer.*Job ID JR\d{6}.*\.pdf$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Desktop\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Screening Serpens Hiring Portal Lure Archive
id: 4b8c2e15-d6f3-4e1a-9a7c-5e2f8b3d917a
description: Detects creation of the Hiring Portal.zip archive used as the Screening Serpens (UNC1549) MiniUpdate/MiniJunk V2 spear-phishing lure (Unit 42, May 2026).
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tracking-iran-apt-screening-serpens/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/23
tags:
  - attack.t1566.001
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_archive:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\Hiring Portal.zip'
      - '\Hiring_Portal.zip'
      - '\HiringPortal.zip'
  selection_pdf:
    TargetFilename|re: '(?i).*(Software|Senior|Principal).*Engineer.*Job ID JR\d{6}.*\.pdf$'
  user_paths:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\Downloads\'
      - '\Desktop\'
      - '\Temp\'
  condition: (selection_archive or selection_pdf) and user_paths
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR email.proofpoint OR email.mimecast OR office365) (@TargetFilename:(*\\Hiring\ Portal.zip OR *\\Hiring_Portal.zip OR *\\HiringPortal.zip) OR @attachment.filename:("Hiring Portal.zip" OR Hiring_Portal.zip OR HiringPortal.zip) OR @email.subject:(*Hiring\ Portal* OR *Job\ Requisition* OR *JR205894*) OR @TargetFilename:(*Software\ Engineer*Job\ ID\ JR* OR *Senior*Engineer*Job\ ID\ JR*))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| (TargetFileName=/\\Hiring[\s_]?Portal\.zip$/i OR TargetFileName=/(Software|Senior|Principal).*Engineer.*Job ID JR\d{6}.*\.pdf$/i)
| TargetFileName=/\\(Downloads|Desktop|Temp)\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Email.src_user) as sender values(All_Email.recipient) as recipient values(All_Email.subject) as subject from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.file_name="Hiring Portal.zip" OR All_Email.file_name="Hiring_Portal.zip" OR All_Email.subject IN ("*Hiring Portal*","*Job Requisition*","*JR2058*") by All_Email.message_id All_Email.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | append [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name IN ("Hiring Portal.zip","Hiring_Portal.zip") OR (Filesystem.file_name="*Job ID JR*.pdf" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\Downloads\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Email.src_user) as sender values(All_Email.recipient) as recipient values(All_Email.subject) as subject from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.file_name="Hiring Portal.zip" OR All_Email.file_name="Hiring_Portal.zip" OR All_Email.subject IN ("*Hiring Portal*","*Job Requisition*","*JR2058*") by All_Email.message_id All_Email.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | append [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name IN ("Hiring Portal.zip","Hiring_Portal.zip") OR (Filesystem.file_name="*Job ID JR*.pdf" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\Downloads\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`]
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("business-startup.org", "buisness-centeral-transportation.com", "premierhealthadvisory.com", "ramiltonsfinance.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["business-startup.org", "buisness-centeral-transportation.com", "premierhealthadvisory.com", "ramiltonsfinance.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain

status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control

    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'

    selection_domain:

falsepositives:

Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Group-policy-managed extension whitelists
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

let BadHashes = dynamic(["44f4f7aca7f1d9bfdaf7b3736934cbe19f851a707662f8f0b0c49b383e054250", "332ba2f0297dfb1599adecc3e9067893e7cf243aa23aedce4906a4c480574c17", "0db36a04d304ad96f9e6f97b531934594cd95a5cea9ff2c9af249201089dc864", "38bd137c672bd58d08c4f0502f993a6561e2c3411773d1ae57ee0151a0a9d11d", "d4a7e9f107fe40c1a5d0139c6c6e25bf6bf57f61feff090bee28f476bb3cc3c2", "bc3b44154518c5794ce639108e7b9c5fecb0c189607a26de1aaed518d890c7ad", "74882085db2088356ed7f72f01e0404a0a98cda88ef56fb15ce74c1f36b26d27", "9cf029daca89523d917dafed0568d11d00e45ec96b5b90b4a1f7fd4018c7da84", "b19e06da580cf91691eda066ac9ee4b09c6e5dc26c367af12660fe1f9306eec4", "8808c794c24367438f183e4be941876f1d3ecd0c8d2eb43b10d2380841d2283b", "43dc62cef52ebdd69e79f10015b3e13890f26c058325c0ff139c70f8d8eadcfa", "9e4a658e6d831c9e9bdfe11884a75b7c64812ed0a80e8495ddf6b316505acac1"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Paved With Intent: ROADtools and Nation-State Tactics in the Cloud

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-05-22 11 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Open-source framework ROADtools is being misused by threat actors for cloud intrusions. Learn how to identify its malicious use. The post Paved With Intent: ROADtools and Nation-State Tactics in the Cloud appeared first on Unit 42 .

ATT&CKT1087 T1098.005 T1190 T1528 T1550 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] UTA0355 device-code phishing: deviceCode auth flow with cross-IP token redemption · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Curious Serpens / APT29 ROADtools-pattern: device registration immediately following non-interactive token acquisition · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ROADtools roadtx FOCI client-ID swap: refresh-token resource hop across MS Office FOCI app IDs
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Curious Serpens / APT29 ROADtools-pattern: device registration immediately following non-interactive token acquisition AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the ROADtools roadtx device-registration sequence where an Entra ID device is registered (T1098.005) shortly after a non-interactive token grant — the pattern Microsoft attributed to Midnight Blizzard / Curious Serpens. Catches attacker-controlled devices being joined as a persistence foothold after token theft. Rationale: Article ties Cloaked Ursa/APT29 and Curious Serpens to ROADtools device-registration persistence (T1098.005). The roadtx module registers devices using one of the public FOCI client IDs (Azure CLI 04b07795, Azure PowerShell 1b730954, Microsoft Office d3590ed6) via non-interactive token flows — joining that to the Audit-Log device add within 30 minutes from a different IP catches the attacker-device persistence pattern. Cross-checked Microsoft Threat Intel reporting on Midnight Blizzard ROADtools usage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2022/08/24/magicweb-nobeliums-post-compromise-trick-to-authenticate-as-anyone/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/005/ • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2025/04/22/phishing-for-codes-russian-threat-actors-target-microsoft-365-oauth-workflows/
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1550
Data sourcesAuthentication Change
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employee enrolling a new corporate laptop while still authenticated from their old machine over VPN
  • Intune autopilot device join initiated by an IT admin from a different jump-host IP than the end-user's
  • BYOD onboarding where the user authenticates from home and the device check-in occurs over the corporate proxy
  • Conditional Access remediation flows that re-register a device after a compliance reset
  • Test-tenant red-team exercises that legitimately use ROADtools
Suppression filter
| where not(UserAgent has_any ("Microsoft-Windows-AzureAd", "MSAL.NetCore", "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Microsoft Windows 10.0")) | where not(ClientAppUsed == "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients" and OperationName == "Add device" and ActorIp startswith "10.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the AAD device object (Get-MgDevice) for the newly-registered device — check displayName, operatingSystem, trustType, and registeredOwners. Pivot on the actor UPN's last 24h SigninLogs to confirm geographic / ASN consistency. 2) Contain: in Entra ID admin center disable the device, revoke all sessions for the user (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset, and require MFA re-registration. 3) Hunt: query CloudAppEvents and OfficeActivity for the actor UPN in the 24h window post-registration looking for MailItemsAccessed, FileDownloaded, eDiscovery searches, or new app-consent grants. Pivot the offending IP against AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs for other UPNs hit by the same source.
let DeviceReg = AuditLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where OperationName has_any ("Add registered owner to device", "Add registered users to device", "Add device") | extend TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName) | extend ActorUpn = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName) | extend ActorIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress) | project RegTime = TimeGenerated, ActorUpn, ActorIp, OperationName, TargetResources; let TokenAuth = AADSignInEventsBeta | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where IsInteractive == false | where ResourceDisplayName in ("Microsoft Graph", "Azure Active Directory Graph", "Windows Azure Active Directory") | where ApplicationId in ("1b730954-1685-4b74-9bfd-dac224a7b894", "d3590ed6-52b3-4102-aeff-aad2292ab01c", "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46") | project AuthTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, UserAgent, ApplicationId, ClientAppUsed; DeviceReg | join kind=inner TokenAuth on $left.ActorUpn == $right.AccountUpn | where datetime_diff('minute', RegTime, AuthTime) between (0 .. 30) | where ActorIp != IPAddress | project RegTime, AuthTime, MinutesBetween = datetime_diff('minute', RegTime, AuthTime), ActorUpn, RegIp = ActorIp, TokenIp = IPAddress, UserAgent, ApplicationId, ClientAppUsed

UTA0355 device-code phishing: deviceCode auth flow with cross-IP token redemption AIDelivery High
Hunts for the UTA0355 (Volexity, 2025) targeted phishing TTP where a victim is sent a device-code prompt and the resulting token is redeemed from attacker infrastructure. ROADtools' roadtx module supports the device_code flow natively; the cross-IP redemption (different IP between code issuance and token use) is the high-fidelity signal. Rationale: Article explicitly cites Volexity's UTA0355 device-code phishing campaign and notes roadtx's device_code flow support. Device-code authentication is rare in normal user populations and a multi-IP redemption inside a 15-minute window is a near-textbook indicator of phished-code abuse — Volexity called this exact pattern out as the UTA0355 IoC. Cross-checked Volexity's April 2025 report. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2025/04/22/phishing-for-codes-russian-threat-actors-target-microsoft-365-oauth-workflows/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/ • https://github.com/dirkjanm/ROADtools
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Conference-room shared device sign-in where a user types a code from their phone (legitimate device-code flow, but typically same network)
  • IT admin demoing device-code flow during training
  • Smart-TV / Apple-TV style sign-in to corporate streaming apps
  • User on mobile network completing device-code on laptop simultaneously (legit cross-IP, same person)
  • Penetration test or purple-team exercise
Suppression filter
| where not(SrcCountries has_any (dynamic(["US","US"])) and array_length(SrcCountries) == 1) | where not(UAs has "Microsoft.WindowsAzureMediaServices")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SigninLogs records for the UPN, examine AuthenticationDetails and CorrelationId. Confirm the device-code issuance IP vs redemption IP — geo, ASN, ISP. Check the user's mailbox for an inbound message containing https://microsoft.com/devicelogin or a Teams chat with that URL in the 30 minutes before code issuance. 2) Contain: Revoke-MgUserSignInSession for the UPN, disable all refresh tokens, force interactive MFA re-auth, block the redemption IP at the Conditional Access named-location level. 3) Hunt: pivot the redemption IP across SigninLogs for other UPNs; check AuditLogs for device-add, app-consent, or mailbox-rule events under that UPN in the next 6 hours.

ROADtools roadtx FOCI client-ID swap: refresh-token resource hop across MS Office FOCI app IDs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for roadtx's signature behaviour of exchanging a refresh token issued to one Microsoft Family of Client IDs (FOCI) app for an access token on a different FOCI app — a defense-evasion trick to broaden token scope without re-prompting MFA. Detection identifies the same refresh-token correlation hitting multiple FOCI app IDs within a short window. Rationale: Article describes roadtx exploiting OAuth on-behalf-of and refresh-token reuse to enable persistence and broaden access; this matches the publicly-documented FOCI refresh-token hopping behaviour (Secureworks, Microsoft research). Detecting >=3 distinct FOCI client IDs sharing refresh-token continuity in <10 minutes for one UPN is high-fidelity for roadtx token replay. Cross-checked Secureworks FOCI research and dirkjanm/ROADtools GitHub. Cross-checked against: • https://www.secureworks.com/research/family-of-client-ids • https://github.com/dirkjanm/ROADtools • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/001/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1606.002
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user on Windows logging into Outlook, OneDrive, Teams, and Edge in quick succession after a fresh sign-in (legit FOCI SSO)
  • IT pilot of new Microsoft 365 app rollouts where users authenticate to many M365 endpoints in sequence
  • Mobile-device enrollment flows where Authenticator App, Intune Company Portal, and Office hit Graph back-to-back
  • Browser-based passwordless flow where Edge proxies tokens to several MS apps
  • Service-account driven automation that exercises multiple Graph scopes
Suppression filter
| where not(UAs has_any ("Microsoft.WindowsAzureMediaServices", "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Microsoft Windows 10.0", "Microsoft Office", "OneDrive")) | where not(array_length(SrcIPs) == 1 and SrcIPs has_any (dynamic(["10.","172.16.","192.168."])))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the burst's SrcIPs and UserAgents — single-IP non-Microsoft UA strings (curl, python-requests, MSAL Python) on a desktop UPN is highly suspicious. Pull CorrelationId and trace the parent token chain in SigninLogs. 2) Contain: Revoke-MgUserSignInSession, invalidate refresh tokens, and apply a Conditional Access policy requiring compliant-device for the offending UPN. 3) Hunt: pivot UserAgent and IPAddress across SigninLogs for other UPNs exhibiting the same multi-FOCI burst; check AuditLogs for application-consent grants, new service-principal credentials, and Exchange mailbox-rule additions in the 24h window.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OpenSSH reverse port-forward (-R) launched on a workstation - Cloud Atlas backup C2 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
