PowerShell-parented taskkill of winrar.exe (Cloud Atlas LNK anti-forensic cleanup) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Step 6 'process concealment' action in the Fixed.ps1 loader chain - PowerShell spawning taskkill.exe /F /IM winrar.exe immediately after the LNK-launched stager extracts the decoy PDF. This pairing is highly article-specific and uncommon outside attacker cleanup routines. Rationale: Anchored on the exact Step 6 string from the article's Fixed.ps1 action table: 'taskkill.exe /F /Im winrar.exe' with PowerShell as parent. Cross-checked Cloud Atlas (aka Inception) on MITRE ATT&CK G0100 confirms loader pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0100/ • https://securelist.com/cloud-atlas/68083/
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1562.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT helpdesk scripts that close hung WinRAR instances via PowerShell remote sessions
  • Endpoint management tools (PDQ Deploy/SCCM) running PowerShell cleanup that kills GUI archivers before silent install
  • Developer build scripts wrapping 7z/WinRAR and force-terminating the GUI on failure
  • Forensic-acquisition scripts that ensure WinRAR isn't holding evidence file handles
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("PDQDeployRunner.exe", "ccmexec.exe", "MsMpEng.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\CCM"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !contains "PDQ"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the PowerShell parent's full command line and InitiatingProcessParentFileName - confirm it traces back to an LNK launch from %TEMP% or a user-downloaded ZIP and not from svc/sysadmin context. Inspect the host for $temp\fixed.ps1, $temp\rar.zip, and *.pdf.lnk artefacts. 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response or EDR network containment; collect $temp, %APPDATA%, and the user's Pictures folder (PowerShower drop path) before reboot. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same AccountName for HKCU\...\Run\YandexBrowser_setup registry creation, googleearth.ps1 in Pictures, and outbound traffic to the article IOC IPs (194.102.104.207, 46.17.45.x, 185.22.154.73).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "taskkill.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "winrar.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/F", "/IM")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "powershell.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\taskkill.exe"
| where CommandLine contains "winrar.exe"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: PowerShell spawning taskkill against winrar.exe (Cloud Atlas anti-forensic)
id: 8a3e3c9c-1d5f-4d1a-9e9b-1c0c8c4a7e11
description: Detects PowerShell parent process spawning taskkill.exe targeting winrar.exe - Cloud Atlas Fixed.ps1 loader cleanup step 6.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/cloud-atlas-2026/119895/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/23
tags:
  - attack.t1070.004
  - attack.t1562.001
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith: '\taskkill.exe'
    ParentImage|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains: 'winrar.exe'
  selection_flags:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/F'
      - '/IM'
  condition: selection_img and selection_cmd and selection_flags
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\taskkill.exe OR *\\TASKKILL.EXE) @CommandLine:(*winrar.exe* OR *WinRAR.exe* OR *WINRAR.EXE*) @ParentImage:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\taskkill\.exe$/i ParentBaseFileName=/powershell\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)winrar\\.exe", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)\\s/(F|IM)\\s", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=taskkill.exe Processes.process="*winrar.exe*" Processes.parent_process_name=powershell.exe by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process, "(?i)/F") OR match(process, "(?i)/IM") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=taskkill.exe Processes.process="*winrar.exe*" Processes.parent_process_name=powershell.exe by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process, "(?i)/F") OR match(process, "(?i)/IM") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
PowerShower dropped to user Pictures folder as googleearth.ps1 AIInstallation High
Hunts the documented PowerShower install path 'C:\Users\[username]\Pictures\googleearth.ps1' - an unusual location/name combination Cloud Atlas uses to hide its reconnaissance/Kerberoasting backdoor. Catches both the file-drop event and subsequent PowerShell execution. Rationale: Direct quote from article: 'PowerShower is dropped onto the system via the path C:\Users\[username]\Pictures\googleearth.ps1.' Filename + path combo is uniquely Cloud Atlas - Google Earth doesn't ship a .ps1 and Pictures isn't a normal script location. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0441/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.powershower
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1547.001 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately syncing a script named googleearth.ps1 via OneDrive/Dropbox into their Pictures folder (rare)
  • Photography or GIS hobbyist scripting Google Earth automation and naming files in Pictures
  • Internal red-team exercise emulating Cloud Atlas using the same IOC paths
  • Backup software previewing/restoring a previously-infected file
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Google\\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe", "Dropbox.exe", "GoogleDriveFS.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped googleearth.ps1 (MD5 against article IOC list 5329f7bff9d0d5db28821b86c26d628f, 7a95360b7e0eb5b107a3d231abbc541a, c0d1eaa15a2cefbab9735787575c8d8e, d5b38b252cf212a4a32763de36732d40, 3c75cedb1196df5eab91f31411ed4b33, 42ac350bfbc5b4eb0fedba16c81919c7, 493b901d1b33eb577db64aadd948f9ce). Confirm the script contains PowerShower indicators (process enumeration, AD admin group queries, Kerberoasting). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the parent PowerShell, delete the .ps1, and remove HKCU\...\Run\YandexBrowser_setup. Reset any AD account that logged on during the dwell window. 3) Hunt: cross-org search for googleearth.ps1 in Pictures, Kerberoast SPN-request bursts from the same account (4769 with RC4 ticket encryption), and outbound to article C2 (tenkoff.org, cloudguide.in, goverru.com, kufar.org, ultimatecore.net, onedrivesupport.net).
union
(DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "googleearth.ps1"
  | where ProcessCommandLine has @"\Pictures\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has @"\Pictures\"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, EventKind="Process", FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where FileName =~ "googleearth.ps1"
  | where FolderPath has @"\Pictures\"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, EventKind="FileDrop", FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine contains "googleearth.ps1"
| where CommandLine contains "Pictures"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

SAM/SECURITY registry hives copied from VSS shadow to Public\Documents as .pdf AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the PowerShower credential grabber: a Volume Shadow Copy is created and SAM/SECURITY hives are copied to C:\Users\Public\Documents\ disguised with a .pdf extension. The combination of HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy source paths, Public\Documents destination, and .pdf masquerade is unique to this article. Rationale: Article states verbatim: 'Copies the SAM (stores local user password hashes) and SECURITY system files from this shadow copy to C:\Users\Public\Documents\, disguising them as PDF files.' The triple constraint (Public\Documents + .pdf + SAM/SECURITY/shadow-copy reference) collapses FP rate to near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/002/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.powershower
ATT&CKT1003.002 T1003.004 T1006 T1036.008
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/Acronis backup agents creating shadow copies and staging files in Public\Documents (won't match SAM/SECURITY filter)
  • Sysadmin running a SAM/SECURITY backup test in a documented IR engagement
  • Disaster-recovery script copying registry hives to a known location (legit, but rare path choice)
  • Security tooling (Velociraptor, KAPE) collecting hives - usually goes to %ProgramData% not Public\Documents
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe", "acrocmd.exe", "AcronisAgent.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !contains "KAPE"
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("services.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full PowerShell parent chain and look for the fodhelper.exe UAC-bypass parent (DeviceProcessEvents InitiatingProcessParentFileName == fodhelper.exe). Inspect C:\Users\Public\Documents\ for *.pdf files whose magic bytes are 'regf' (registry hive). 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, treat ALL local accounts and the logged-on domain account as compromised, force enterprise password rotation for that user and any cached creds, revoke Kerberos TGTs (krbtgt rotation if domain controller affected). 3) Hunt: search for fodhelper.exe spawning PowerShell across the fleet, Kerberoast SPN requests from the same account, and outbound exfil to article C2 IPs/domains. Pivot on any other host in the same OU.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\Users\Public\Documents\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".pdf" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ".pdf"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("SAM", "SECURITY", "HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy", "Win32_ShadowCopy", "vssadmin")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("SAM", "SECURITY", "HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy", "Win32_ShadowCopy", "vssadmin")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "cmd.exe", "wmic.exe", "fodhelper.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine contains "Public\\Documents"
| where CommandLine contains ".pdf"
| where CommandLine has_any ("SAM", "SECURITY", "HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy", "Win32_ShadowCopy", "vssadmin")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: SAM/SECURITY hive exfil-staged in Public Documents as PDF (Cloud Atlas PowerShower)
id: a1b2c3d4-e5f6-4789-9012-345678901234
description: Detects command lines copying SAM or SECURITY hives from a VSS shadow copy to C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents with a .pdf masquerade extension.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/23
tags:

  - attack.t1003.004

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  dest_path:
    CommandLine|contains: '\Users\Public\Documents\'
  hive_ref:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'SAM'
      - 'SECURITY'
      - 'HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy'
  pdf_mask:
    CommandLine|contains: '.pdf'
  condition: dest_path and hive_ref and pdf_mask
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:(*\\Public\\Documents\\* OR *\\PUBLIC\\DOCUMENTS\\*) @CommandLine:*.pdf* (@CommandLine:*SAM* OR @CommandLine:*SECURITY* OR @CommandLine:*HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy* OR @CommandLine:*vssadmin*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| regex("(?i)\\\\Users\\\\Public\\\\Documents\\\\", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)\\.pdf", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)(SAM|SECURITY|HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy|Win32_ShadowCopy|vssadmin)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*Public\\Documents*" Processes.process="*.pdf*" (Processes.process="*SAM*" OR Processes.process="*SECURITY*" OR Processes.process="*HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*Public\\Documents*" Processes.process="*.pdf*" (Processes.process="*SAM*" OR Processes.process="*SECURITY*" OR Processes.process="*HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
termsrv.dll patched (multi-RDP enabling) - takeown + binary write + TermService restart AIInstallation High
Hunts Cloud Atlas's rdp_new.ps1 (MD5 1a11b26dd0261ef27a112ce8b361c247) which takes ownership of termsrv.dll, patches the 39 81 3C 06 00 00 byte sequence to B8 00 01 00 00 89 81 38 06 00 00 90 to allow concurrent RDP sessions, then restarts TermService. Lets attacker share the host invisibly with the legit user. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact script name (rdp_new.ps1, MD5 1a11b26dd0261ef27a112ce8b361c247), the unique target file (termsrv.dll), the documented takeown+permissions+patch+restart chain, and the verbatim byte-pattern sequences in code blocks [1] and [2]. termsrv.dll modification outside of Windows Update/TrustedInstaller is exceedingly rare. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/001/ • https://github.com/stascorp/rdpwrap
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112 T1021.001 T1547.014
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • RDPWrap installation by an admin to enable concurrent sessions on a non-server SKU (same TTP, different actor)
  • Windows feature-update where termsrv.dll is replaced by TrustedInstaller (excluded by parent filter)
  • IT engineer troubleshooting Remote Desktop Services and restarting TermService
  • Pen-test tooling that explicitly modifies termsrv.dll for ATT&CK emulation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe", "TiWorker.exe", "msiexec.exe", "wuauclt.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\WinSxS\\"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\servicing\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash termsrv.dll against the Microsoft-signed catalog for the OS build (sigcheck -h -c C:\Windows\System32\termsrv.dll) - any unsigned/altered hash is positive. Pull rdp_new.ps1 (MD5 1a11b26dd0261ef27a112ce8b361c247) from the host. Check fDenyTSConnections=0 and MaxInstanceCount registry changes. 2) Contain: isolate via EDR, restore termsrv.dll from a clean baseline (sfc /scannow then dism /restorehealth, or robocopy from a peer system), restart TermService, force-disconnect any active RDP sessions, reset the user and any admin accounts that logged on. 3) Hunt: search for the byte pattern '39 81 3C 06 00 00' replacement across the fleet via EDR YARA, look for ssh.exe with -R flag (reverse tunnel UC), and outbound to article IOC IPs.
let TermsrvProc = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "termsrv.dll"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("takeown", "icacls", "TermService", "Restart-Service", "Stop-Service", "net stop termservice", "sc ")
        or FileName in~ ("takeown.exe", "icacls.exe")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, EventKind="Proc", FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let TermsrvFileWrite = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where FolderPath endswith @"\System32" and FileName =~ "termsrv.dll"
    | where ActionType in ("FileModified", "FileCreated", "FileRenamed")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe", "msiexec.exe", "TiWorker.exe")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, EventKind="FileWrite", FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
union TermsrvProc, TermsrvFileWrite
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine contains "termsrv.dll"
| where CommandLine has_any ("takeown", "icacls", "TermService", "Restart-Service", "Stop-Service")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

OpenSSH reverse port-forward (-R) launched on a workstation - Cloud Atlas backup C2 AICommand & Control High
Hunts the reverse SSH tunnel installer Cloud Atlas drops via PsExec/PAExec: VBS scripts launch ssh.exe with -R to expose the victim's internal port to an attacker-controlled server. Detection focuses on ssh.exe with the -R flag on Windows endpoints where SSH client use is not part of the normal admin workflow. Rationale: Article: 'To install a reverse SSH tunnel on a victim's host, the attackers run VBS scripts via PAExec or PsExec.' The -R flag is the canonical reverse-port-forward switch; combining it with VBS/PsExec parents removes the noise from legitimate developer/admin SSH use. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090/001/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090.001 T1219 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network/sysadmin using ssh -R to set up jump-host access for legitimate remote management (typically from a known admin workstation, not VBS-spawned)
  • Developer running ssh -R for ngrok-like service exposure during local development
  • Cloud automation tool (Ansible, Terraform) using SSH reverse tunnels for callback (parent would be Python/Ansible, not wscript)
  • Internal Linux-on-Windows WSL workflows that invoke ssh.exe (typically interactive shell parent)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Git\\"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Users\\" or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe", "WindowsTerminal.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine !contains "github.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the full ssh.exe command line and the -R argument target (host:port). Geo-lookup the destination - article IOC IPs are 194.102.104.207, 46.17.45.49/56, 46.17.44.125/212, 185.22.154.73, 194.87.196.163, 195.58.49.9. Pull the parent VBS script body (likely under %TEMP% or C:\Windows\Temp) and the PsExec/PAExec command line that staged it. 2) Contain: kill the ssh.exe PID, isolate the host, block the destination IP at the egress firewall, revoke any private keys present in %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\ and rotate matching authorized_keys on attacker-suspected servers. 3) Hunt: pivot on PsExec/PAExec service installations (event 7045 + service name length 1-2 chars) across the domain, search for the patched OpenSSH binary hash, and look for additional outbound :22/:443 connections to article IOC IP ranges.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "ssh.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-R\s+\S+"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "psexec.exe", "psexec64.exe", "paexec.exe", "services.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "ssh.exe"
    | where RemotePort == 22 or RemotePort == 443
    | project NetTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
  ) on DeviceName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\ssh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-R\s+\S+"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "PsExec.exe", "paexec.exe", "services.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: OpenSSH reverse port-forward on Windows endpoint (Cloud Atlas backup C2)
id: c3d4e5f6-a7b8-4901-c234-567890123456
description: Detects ssh.exe launched with the -R (reverse port forward) flag on Windows hosts spawned by a script interpreter or PsExec/PAExec - Cloud Atlas backup C2 via patched OpenSSH.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/cloud-atlas-2026/119895/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/23
tags:
  - attack.t1572
  - attack.t1090.001
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith: '\ssh.exe'
  selection_flag:
    CommandLine|contains: ' -R '
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\PsExec.exe'
      - '\paexec.exe'
      - '\services.exe'
  condition: selection_img and selection_flag and selection_parent
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\ssh.exe OR *\\SSH.EXE OR *\\Ssh.exe) @CommandLine:"* -R *" @ParentImage:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\WSCRIPT.EXE OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\CSCRIPT.EXE OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\PsExec.exe OR *\\PSEXEC.EXE OR *\\paexec.exe OR *\\PAExec.exe OR *\\services.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\ssh\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)\\s-R\\s+\\S+", field=CommandLine)
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(wscript|cscript|cmd|powershell|pwsh|psexec|psexec64|paexec|services)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=ssh.exe Processes.process="* -R *" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(parent_process_name, "(?i)^(wscript|cscript|cmd|powershell|psexec|paexec|services)\.exe$") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=ssh.exe Processes.process="* -R *" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(parent_process_name, "(?i)^(wscript|cscript|cmd|powershell|psexec|paexec|services)\.exe$") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2018-0802")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2018-0802")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("fixed.ps1", "termsrv.dll", "winrar.exe", "video.vbs", "googleearth.ps1", "fodhelper.exe", "rdp_new.ps1", "gen.vbs", "writetoschedulergeneratekey.vbs", "run.vbs", "writetoschedulerrunssh.vbs", "kill.vbs", "writetoschedulerkillssh.vbs", "libcrypto.dll", "syruntime.dll") or FolderPath has_any ("C:\Users\Public\Documents\", "C:\Windows\ime", "C:\Windows\System32\ime", "C:\Windows\pla", "C:\Windows\inf"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

DeviceFileEvents

          InitiatingProcessCommandLine

Foul play: Fake FIFA websites target soccer fans looking for World Cup tickets, merchandise

ESET WeLiveSecurity
2026-05-22 6 use cases 1 technique 3 kill-chain phases detected

Watch out for bogus World Cup websites that mimic official ticket and merchandise flows to steal money and personal data

Domainsfifa26.shop fifaworldcup26.hospitality.fifa.com

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Mail-borne click to fake FIFA World Cup 2026 phishing domain · [LLM] Endpoint DNS or web traffic to fake FIFA World Cup 2026 typosquat domain · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Mail-borne click to fake FIFA World Cup 2026 phishing domain AIDelivery High
Detects users clicking links in email that resolve to known FIFA World Cup 2026 typosquat domains (fifa26.shop, *26-fifa.com and lookalike patterns). Pivots on Safe Links / email URL telemetry to catch the delivery vector before credential entry. Rationale: Uses the article's named IOC fifa26.shop plus the second sample family `*26-fifa[.]com`, expanded to a typosquat regex covering common .shop/.store TLDs the article explicitly calls out. Explicit allow for legitimate fifa.com prevents official-site collisions. Cross-checked: WHOIS/abuse.ch lookups for typosquat campaigns around major sporting events show recurring `<event>+<year>+.shop` patterns. Sentinel rewritten to use ImWebSession (EmailEvents/EmailUrlInfo are M365D-only and not in this tenant's Sentinel schema). Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web Email.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate fan news sites or blogs whose path contains 'fifa' and '2026'
  • Official FIFA marketing redirects through partner shorteners
  • Sports journalists researching scam sites for stories
  • Security researchers / TI analysts visiting the IOCs for triage
  • Sponsored ad clicks to FIFA official partners on non-.fifa.com domains (e.g. ticketing resellers explicitly authorised by FIFA)
Suppression filter
| where not (Url matches regex @'(?i)://(www\.)?fifa\.com(/|$)') and not (HttpHostName endswith 'fifa.com') and not (HttpHostName in~ ('store.fifa.com','tickets.fifa.com','hospitality.fifa.com'))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the URL host is not a legitimate FIFA partner (FIFA's only official ticketing channels are fifa.com/tickets, fifa.com/hospitality, and the Qatar Airways travel packages). Pull the originating email (NetworkMessageId) or referrer to identify delivery vector. 2) Contain: block the typosquat domain at proxy/DNS and Safe Links, purge any related emails via M365 Threat Explorer, force password reset + revoke sessions for the clicking user (article confirms credential + card harvesting). 3) Hunt: pivot on the user's last 24h for additional FIFA-themed clicks, look for outbound POSTs to the same host (likely contains exfiltrated card data), and scan EmailUrlInfo for the same UrlDomain across other recipients in the org.
let TyposquatRegex = @'(?i)(fifa.*(26|2026|worldcup)|(26|2026|worldcup).*fifa)';
let KnownBad = dynamic(['fifa26.shop','26-fifa.com']);
let ClickedUrls = UrlClickEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where ActionType in ('ClickAllowed','ClickedThrough','UrlScanInProgress')
  | where Url matches regex TyposquatRegex or parse_url(Url).Host has_any (KnownBad)
  | where not (Url matches regex @'(?i)://(www\.)?fifa\.com(/|$)');
ClickedUrls
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | project NetworkMessageId, UrlDomain, MailUrl=Url) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Url, MailUrl, UrlDomain, ActionType, ThreatTypes, NetworkMessageId, IPAddress, IsClickedThrough
| order by Timestamp desc
let TyposquatRegex = @'(?i)(fifa.*(26|2026|worldcup)|(26|2026|worldcup).*fifa)';
let KnownBad = dynamic(['fifa26.shop','26-fifa.com']);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(Url)
| where Url matches regex TyposquatRegex or HttpHostName has_any (KnownBad)
| where not (Url matches regex @'(?i)://(www\.)?fifa\.com(/|$)') and not (HttpHostName endswith 'fifa.com')
| extend MailReferrer = iif(HttpRequestHeaderReferer matches regex @'(?i)(outlook|mail\.google|webmail|owa|m365|office\.com)', true, false)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, SrcHostname, DstHostname, Url, HttpHostName, HttpRequestHeaderReferer, MailReferrer, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Click or Navigation to Fake FIFA World Cup 2026 Typosquat Domain
id: 7c0e1f4a-8a6f-4f3d-9b1a-2f8c1d3e4b91
description: Detects browser navigation to known fake FIFA World Cup 2026 phishing domains and typosquat patterns reported by ESET.
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/cybersecurity/foul-play-fake-fifa-world-cup-websites-tickets/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/23
tags:
  - attack.t1566.002
  - attack.t1583.001
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: proxy
detection:
  selection_known:
    c-uri|contains:
      - 'fifa26.shop'
      - '26-fifa.com'
  selection_pattern:
    c-uri|re|i: '(fifa.*(26|2026|worldcup)|(26|2026|worldcup).*fifa)\.(shop|store|online|xyz|top|site|com)'
  filter_legit:
    c-uri|contains:
      - 'fifa.com/'
      - '.fifa.com'
  condition: (selection_known or selection_pattern) and not filter_legit
level: high
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate fan blogs or news sites with 'fifa' and '2026' in the URL path
  - Marketing redirects from official FIFA partners
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3) AND (@DestinationHostname:(*fifa26.shop* OR *26-fifa.* OR *26fifa.*) OR @QueryName:(*fifa26.shop* OR *26-fifa.* OR *26fifa.*)) AND NOT @DestinationHostname:(*.fifa.com OR fifa.com)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/(?i)(fifa.*(26|2026|worldcup)|(26|2026|worldcup).*fifa)\.(shop|store|online|xyz|top|site|com)/ OR DomainName=/(?i)^(fifa26\.shop|26-fifa\.com)$/
| NOT DomainName=/(?i)\.fifa\.com$|^fifa\.com$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=[count(), min(@timestamp), max(@timestamp)])
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.user) as user values(Web.http_referrer) as referrer values(Web.url) as url from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*fifa26.shop*" OR Web.url="*26-fifa.*" OR Web.url="*fifa*worldcup*" Web.url IN ("*.shop/*","*.store/*","*.online/*","*.xyz/*","*.top/*")) AND NOT (Web.url="*fifa.com/*" OR Web.url="*fifa.com.*") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest Web.url Web.http_referrer | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")` | where match(referrer, "(?i)(mail|outlook|gmail|owa|webmail|m365)") OR isnull(referrer) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.user) as user values(Web.http_referrer) as referrer values(Web.url) as url from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*fifa26.shop*" OR Web.url="*26-fifa.*" OR Web.url="*fifa*worldcup*" Web.url IN ("*.shop/*","*.store/*","*.online/*","*.xyz/*","*.top/*")) AND NOT (Web.url="*fifa.com/*" OR Web.url="*fifa.com.*") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest Web.url Web.http_referrer | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")` | where match(referrer, "(?i)(mail|outlook|gmail|owa|webmail|m365)") OR isnull(referrer) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
Endpoint DNS or web traffic to fake FIFA World Cup 2026 typosquat domain AIDelivery High
Detects endpoint DNS resolution or outbound web connection to fake FIFA World Cup 2026 phishing infrastructure (fifa26.shop, *26-fifa.com pattern) regardless of delivery vector — catches users reaching the site via sponsored search, social-media ads, or shared chat links. Rationale: Direct DNS/web pivot using the two domain families named in the article (fifa26.shop and *26-fifa.com), expanded to a tight typosquat regex bounded by the .shop/.store/.online TLDs the article specifically calls out as a red flag. Browser-process filter on the Defender side suppresses background DNS noise. Cross-checked against MITRE T1583.001 (typosquatting subtechnique). Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/
ATT&CKT1566.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat intel / DFIR analysts resolving the IOC during triage from a managed workstation
  • Web crawlers or threat-intel scrapers running in the org's environment
  • Marketing or PR staff researching the campaign for brand-protection write-ups
  • Fan-blog hostnames that legitimately contain 'fifa' + '2026' (rare but possible on .com)
  • Sandbox/VM detonations of malicious URLs from a corporate analyst host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountUpn !in~ ('soc-analyst@contoso.com','threat-intel@contoso.com') and DeviceName !startswith 'SOC-SANDBOX-'
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the requesting process and user — if it's a browser session by a regular employee (not SOC/TI), treat as a real visit; pull DeviceNetworkEvents for the same DeviceId in a ±30min window to see if any POST traffic followed the resolution (indicates credential or card submission). 2) Contain: sinkhole the domain at recursive DNS / block at proxy + Safe Links, isolate device if POST traffic to the typosquat is confirmed, force password reset and card cancellation for the affected user. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host in the org that resolved any matching FIFA typosquat domain in the last 30d, query EmailUrlInfo for the same domains to size the delivery footprint, and pivot on shared resolved IPs to discover sibling typosquat infrastructure on the same hosting.
let TyposquatRegex = @'(?i)(fifa.*(26|2026|worldcup)|(26|2026|worldcup).*fifa)\.(shop|store|online|xyz|top|site|com)';
let KnownBad = dynamic(['fifa26.shop','26-fifa.com']);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend Host = tolower(tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl).Host))
| where Host has_any (KnownBad) or Host matches regex TyposquatRegex
| where not (Host endswith 'fifa.com') and Host != 'fifa.com'
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ('chrome.exe','msedge.exe','firefox.exe','brave.exe','opera.exe','iexplore.exe','safari.exe')
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, Host, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let TyposquatRegex = @'(?i)(fifa.*(26|2026|worldcup)|(26|2026|worldcup).*fifa)\.(shop|store|online|xyz|top|site|com)';
let KnownBad = dynamic(['fifa26.shop','26-fifa.com']);
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Name has_any (KnownBad) or Name matches regex TyposquatRegex
    | where not (Name endswith 'fifa.com') and Name != 'fifa.com'
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, QueryName=Name, QueryType=QueryTypeName, Result, Source='DnsEvents'),
  (ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DnsQuery has_any (KnownBad) or DnsQuery matches regex TyposquatRegex
    | where not (DnsQuery endswith 'fifa.com') and DnsQuery != 'fifa.com'
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, QueryName=DnsQuery, QueryType=DnsQueryTypeName, Result=DnsResponseName, Source='ImDnsActivity')
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 9a4b2d1e-5c8f-4e2a-bb7c-1a9d4e6f2c83
description: Detects DNS resolution of FIFA World Cup 2026 phishing typosquat domains reported by ESET (fifa26.shop and the *26-fifa.com family).
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/23
tags:

  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection_known:
    QueryName|contains:
      - 'fifa26.shop'
      - '26-fifa.com'
      - '26-fifa.'
  selection_pattern:
    QueryName|re|i: '(fifa.*(26|2026|worldcup)|(26|2026|worldcup).*fifa)\.(shop|store|online|xyz|top|site)'
  filter_legit:
    QueryName|endswith:
      - '.fifa.com'
      - 'fifa.com'

  - Legitimate fan sites with 'fifa' and '2026' in the hostname
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22) AND (@QueryName:(*fifa26.shop* OR *26-fifa.* OR *26fifa.* OR fifa*worldcup*.shop OR fifa*worldcup*.store)) AND NOT @QueryName:(*.fifa.com OR fifa.com)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/(?i)^(fifa26\.shop|.*26-fifa\..*|.*26fifa\.(shop|store))$/ OR DomainName=/(?i)(fifa.*(26|2026|worldcup)|(26|2026|worldcup).*fifa)\.(shop|store|online|xyz|top|site)/
| NOT DomainName=/(?i)(^|\.)fifa\.com$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName, IpAddress], function=[count(), min(@timestamp), max(@timestamp)])
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(DNS.src) as src values(DNS.answer) as answer from datamodel=Network_Resolution where (DNS.query="fifa26.shop" OR DNS.query="*.fifa26.shop" OR DNS.query="*26-fifa.com" OR DNS.query="*26-fifa.*" OR DNS.query="*26fifa.shop" OR DNS.query="*fifa*worldcup*.shop" OR DNS.query="*fifa*worldcup*.store") AND NOT (DNS.query="*.fifa.com" OR DNS.query="fifa.com") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name("DNS")` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(DNS.src) as src values(DNS.answer) as answer from datamodel=Network_Resolution where (DNS.query="fifa26.shop" OR DNS.query="*.fifa26.shop" OR DNS.query="*26-fifa.com" OR DNS.query="*26-fifa.*" OR DNS.query="*26fifa.shop" OR DNS.query="*fifa*worldcup*.shop" OR DNS.query="*fifa*worldcup*.store") AND NOT (DNS.query="*.fifa.com" OR DNS.query="fifa.com") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name("DNS")` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Boxlite sandbox writes to SSH authorized_keys (post-exploit RCE pivot) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match

OCI image extraction creates symlink with absolute path target (CWE-61 primitive) AIExploitation High
Detects the Boxlite OCI layer extractor creating symlinks during tar processing where the link target points outside the staging directory (absolute path under /etc, /root, /home, /var/spool/cron, etc.). This is the core CVE-2026-46703 primitive — the unvalidated symlink target in apply_oci_layer() that turns a subsequent regular-file tar entry into an arbitrary host file write. Rationale: Article names the vulnerable binary explicitly (boxlite) and the exploit primitive's effect (writes outside dest staging dir into host paths like /etc/passwd, /root/.ssh/authorized_keys). The detection pivots on these two facts together — a high-fidelity pair because legitimate Boxlite extraction only writes inside its staging directory (typically /tmp/<sandbox-id>/ or /var/lib/boxlite/), never into /etc or /root. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f396-4rp4-7v2j
ATT&CKT1611 T1574 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Boxlite administrator manually copying configuration files into /etc/boxlite/ during install/upgrade
  • Custom Boxlite deployments that legitimately stage images under non-default paths (rare; would warrant tuning)
  • Security researcher locally reproducing the PoC in a contained test VM
  • Boxlite write-access to /var/lib/boxlite/* mis-pathed in the filter (false positive of the filter, not the detection — refine startswith list)
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath startswith "/etc/boxlite/" or FolderPath startswith "/var/lib/boxlite/")
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--install", "--upgrade", "--config-init"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Pull the full SyslogMessage / AdditionalFields for the alert and identify the OCI image digest Boxlite was extracting at the time (search for `extract_layer_tarball_streaming` or registry pull logs from the same host within the prior 5 minutes). Inspect the target path to determine impact (authorized_keys = RCE, /etc/passwd = account takeover, /etc/sudoers.d = privesc). Step 2 (Contain): Stop the boxlite service on the affected host (`systemctl stop boxlite`), quarantine the malicious image hash from the host's image cache, and roll back the modified host file from backup. If /root/.ssh/authorized_keys was touched, rotate SSH keys and audit access. Step 3 (Hunt): Pivot on the OCI image digest across all hosts running Boxlite to find other infected nodes; query registry/proxy logs for the image's pull URL to identify upstream distribution; check for any process executed as root within 60s of the write that may indicate successful RCE.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "boxlite"
| where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated", "SymbolicLinkCreated")
| where FolderPath startswith "/etc/"
   or FolderPath startswith "/root/"
   or FolderPath startswith "/home/"
   or FolderPath startswith "/var/spool/cron/"
   or FolderPath startswith "/etc/cron.d/"
   or FolderPath startswith "/etc/sudoers.d/"
   or FolderPath startswith "/etc/systemd/system/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "boxlite"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("symlink", "symlinkat", "linkat")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/etc/", "/root/", "/home/", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/cron.d", "/etc/sudoers.d", "/etc/systemd/system")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, ProcessID, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Boxlite OCI Extraction Symlink Escape (CVE-2026-46703)
id: a3f8c9e1-7d4b-4f2a-9c1e-8b5d2f6a3c47
description: Detects the Boxlite sandbox extractor creating files in sensitive host paths during OCI image extraction, indicative of CVE-2026-46703 symlink escape exploitation.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f396-4rp4-7v2j
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/22
tags:
  - attack.t1611
  - attack.t1574
logsource:
  product: linux
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '/boxlite'
    TargetFilename|startswith:
      - '/etc/'
      - '/root/.ssh/'
      - '/var/spool/cron/'
      - '/etc/cron.d/'
      - '/etc/sudoers.d/'
      - '/etc/systemd/system/'
  condition: selection
level: high

Boxlite sandbox writes to SSH authorized_keys (post-exploit RCE pivot) AIInstallation High
Detects the Boxlite service writing to any authorized_keys file on the host — the article explicitly calls out this technique as the RCE pivot ('writing the attacker's public key into the host's authorized_keys'). Since Boxlite has no legitimate reason to touch user SSH key files outside its sandboxed Box filesystems, any such write is high-confidence post-exploitation of CVE-2026-46703. Rationale: Article body explicitly cites this technique: 'The attacker can further leverage this capability to achieve remote code execution, such as writing the attacker's public key into the host's authorized_keys.' Boxlite is a container sandbox — it has zero legitimate workflow that involves writing to /root/.ssh/ or /home/*/.ssh/ on the host, making this a clean alerting signal. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f396-4rp4-7v2j
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Boxlite developer running PoC test in isolated lab environment
  • Sysadmin manually mis-using boxlite binary to copy files (extremely unlikely workflow)
  • Boxlite future feature adds legitimate SSH key sharing into Boxes (would require explicit re-tuning)
  • Symlink farms in user home dirs where authorized_keys is a link to a path Boxlite legitimately stages (none observed in default deployments)
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Capture the modified authorized_keys file immediately (`cp /root/.ssh/authorized_keys /tmp/ir-$(date +%s).authkeys`) and diff against the last known-good backup to identify the attacker's pubkey. Note the timestamp and correlate with Boxlite OCI image pulls in the prior 10 minutes — extract the image manifest digest. Step 2 (Contain): Remove the attacker-added pubkey from authorized_keys, kill any active SSH sessions from unknown IPs (`who`, `last`, `ss -tnp`), rotate the user's SSH keys, and block the malicious OCI image hash at the registry / image-pull policy layer. Step 3 (Hunt): Search across the fleet for the same OCI image digest and the same attacker pubkey in authorized_keys files; query egress logs for outbound SSH connections from any host with Boxlite installed in the last 30 days; review Boxlite version inventory and patch to fix for CVE-2026-46703.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "boxlite"
| where FileName =~ "authorized_keys" or FolderPath has "/.ssh/authorized_keys"
| where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "SymbolicLinkCreated")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "boxlite"
| where SyslogMessage has "authorized_keys"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, ProcessID, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b673b4e3400c71bd72464c98610c952e2164f70f946873b82adf3e6212851d54") or SHA1 in~ ("b673b4e3400c71bd72464c98610c952e2164f70f946873b82adf3e6212851d54") or MD5 in~ ("b673b4e3400c71bd72464c98610c952e2164f70f946873b82adf3e6212851d54")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b673b4e3400c71bd72464c98610c952e2164f70f946873b82adf3e6212851d54") or SHA1 in~ ("b673b4e3400c71bd72464c98610c952e2164f70f946873b82adf3e6212851d54") or MD5 in~ ("b673b4e3400c71bd72464c98610c952e2164f70f946873b82adf3e6212851d54")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["b673b4e3400c71bd72464c98610c952e2164f70f946873b82adf3e6212851d54"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable Twig package (CVE-2026-46633) installed (twig/twig < 3.26.0) AIExploitation High
Surface assets where Microsoft Defender TVM reports the Twig PHP templating library at a version vulnerable to CVE-2026-46633. Exploitation gives RCE via single-quote injection in a `{% use %}` template name; SecurityPolicy allows `{% use %}` even under sandbox, so any application that accepts attacker-influenced template names against twig/twig < 3.26.0 is reachable. Prioritise patching to 3.26.0 or later. Rationale: Article is a vendor advisory: identifies the exact package (composer:twig/twig), fixed version (3.26.0), and CVE (CVE-2026-46633). The only high-fidelity, non-generic detection from this content is asset coverage — every other behaviour-based UC (PHP web server spawning shells, web-shell cache file writes) collapses into generic web-shell rules already shipped, which the prompt explicitly excludes. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7p85-w9px-jpjp
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM picks up `twig/twig` development copies in non-production scratch directories (developer laptops) where the dependency is pinned but not exposed externally
  • Lab / sandbox VMs that intentionally host vulnerable packages for security research
  • Vendored or vendored-and-forked copies of Twig embedded inside larger PHP applications (e.g., Symfony, Drupal, Shopware) where the parent product's own patched release supersedes the bundled version but TVM still reports the bundled string
  • Stale TVM scan data on decommissioned hosts that have already been re-imaged but not yet aged out of the inventory table
Suppression filter
// Exclude developer / non-production hosts via MachineGroup tagging
| where DeviceName !has "dev-" and DeviceName !has "-lab"
// Exclude assets tagged as decommissioned in your CMDB join
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the asset is internet-facing or accepts external user input that flows into a Twig template loader (look for application owner in CMDB; check WAF / reverse-proxy logs for the host). Validate the reported `SoftwareVersion` is below 3.26.0 and not a vendored copy already patched by a parent product release. 2. Contain: if internet-facing and unpatched, request an emergency patch ticket to upgrade twig/twig to >= 3.26.0; in the interim, validate that no application surface passes user-controlled strings into `{% use %}` template names and add a WAF rule blocking request bodies containing `{% use '` with a single-quote inside a template name argument. 3. Hunt: pivot to DeviceProcessEvents for the affected host(s) and look for the PHP-FPM / Apache / Nginx process tree spawning `sh`, `bash`, `cmd.exe`, or `powershell.exe` in the past 30 days — any such tree post-dating the vulnerable version's first install is a possible exploitation event worth deeper forensic review.

    or (SoftwareName has "twig" and SoftwareVendor has "twig")

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel desc, DeviceName asc
// CVE-2026-46633 — Twig {% use %} PHP code injection (vuln < 3.26.0)
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId == "CVE-2026-46633"
    or (SoftwareName has "twig" and SoftwareVendor has "twig")
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId, CveId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion,

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel desc, DeviceName asc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity from GitHub OIDC with unexpected repo/branch sub claim

AWS IAM role trust policy created with set-qualified operator on GitHub OIDC sub claim AIInstallation High
Hunts the exact misconfiguration class that @hulumi/policies <1.3.2 failed to flag: CreateRole/UpdateAssumeRolePolicy CloudTrail events whose trust policy uses ForAnyValue:StringLike / ForAllValues:StringLike / ForAllValues:StringEquals against token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub. Any role created with this shape — particularly with wildcards in the sub value — is assumable by GitHub Actions workflows the role owner never intended to authorize. Rationale: Article specifies the exact unsafe pattern: set-qualified operators (ForAnyValue:StringLike etc.) applied to token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub bypass the inspector. CloudTrail's CreateRole/UpdateAssumeRolePolicy carries the full policyDocument as JSON — substring matching for both the operator family AND the OIDC sub claim string is high-fidelity because the combination is essentially never seen in correctly-authored trust policies (canonical pattern is the bare StringLike or StringEquals). Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/avoiding-mistakes-with-aws-oidc-integration-conditions • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition_operators.html • https://docs.github.com/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/configuring-openid-connect-in-amazon-web-services
ATT&CKT1098.003 T1199 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate use of ForAnyValue:StringLike to match the sub claim against a constrained array of specific repo+branch values (e.g. matching exactly two protected branches) — not an actual bypass but matches the query
  • Internal Terraform/CDK modules that templatize trust policies and emit ForAnyValue:StringLike even when only a single sub value is being matched
  • Cross-account/role-consolidation pipelines that intentionally use ForAnyValue:StringLike across a curated allowlist of GitHub repos belonging to the same engineering org
  • DR/test-account replays of role creation as part of disaster-recovery validation (same policy shape, expected event)
Suppression filter
| where NOT match(policyDocument, "(?i)token\.actions\.githubusercontent\.com:sub\"\s*:\s*\[\s*\"repo:[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+/[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+:(ref:refs/heads/[a-zA-Z0-9._/-]+|environment:[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+|pull_request)\"")
Response runbook
Triage: pull the full policyDocument from the CloudTrail event; extract the sub claim values inside the set-qualified operator. If any value contains an unanchored wildcard (`*`, `repo:*`, `repo:org/*:*`) or is missing entirely, treat as confirmed unsafe. Contain: revert the trust policy via UpdateAssumeRolePolicy to the prior known-good version (use CloudTrail's prior policyDocument value), or detach the role temporarily by attaching a Deny-all permissions boundary while you investigate the assumer identity. Hunt: enumerate all sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity calls against this role's ARN for the last 90 days; cross-reference the assumed sub claims against your expected GitHub org/repo allowlist; pivot on any unexpected actor to find downstream AWS API calls made under the assumed credentials.

AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity from GitHub OIDC with unexpected repo/branch sub claim AIExploitation Medium
Downstream hunt for actor abuse of a role whose unsafe trust policy slipped past @hulumi/policies <1.3.2. Pivots on sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity events where the WebIdentity issuer is token.actions.githubusercontent.com and the asserted sub claim does not match the org's approved GitHub repo allowlist — flagging the first-time-seen repo+role pairs that an attacker exploiting a wildcard sub policy would generate. Rationale: The article's bypass directly enables GitHub Actions OIDC sub-claim impersonation against IAM roles. AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is the actor-observable consequence — the userIdentity.userName field on the CloudTrail event carries the asserted sub (e.g. repo:owner/repo:ref:refs/heads/main). Anti-joining against an approved-org/repo lookup is the cleanest baseline-deviation pivot for catching exploitation of an unsafe policy that the scanner missed. Cross-referenced with the AWS GitHub OIDC docs and the Wiz misconfiguration write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/avoiding-mistakes-with-aws-oidc-integration-conditions • https://docs.github.com/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/configuring-openid-connect-in-amazon-web-services
ATT&CKT1199 T1078.004 T1550.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • New legitimate repository onboarding that hasn't been added to the approved_github_oidc_roles lookup yet
  • Fork-based PR workflows where the sub claim format is 'repo:org/repo:pull_request' rather than the usual ref:refs/heads/* pattern
  • Renamed/migrated GitHub repositories where the sub claim now references the new org/name and the lookup is stale
  • Self-hosted GitHub Enterprise instances using a different OIDC issuer URL whose sub claim format diverges from cloud GitHub
  • Reusable workflows invoked from a different upstream repo (sub claim points at the caller, which may be unlisted)
Response runbook
Triage: extract the gh_org/gh_repo/gh_ref tuple from the userIdentity.userName claim and compare to the org's approved repo registry; check the trust policy of the assumed role for the unsafe set-qualified operator pattern from UC1; review the source IP and user-agent (legitimate GitHub Actions runners emit a recognizable UA). Contain: if the assumer is unauthorized, immediately revoke active sessions via `aws iam put-role-policy` attaching a Deny-all inline policy, then rotate the role's trust policy to a strict StringEquals sub claim; if confirmed-malicious, also revoke any short-lived credentials the actor minted via subsequent sts: calls. Hunt: enumerate all AWS API calls performed under the assumed-role session ID for the past 30 days; look for data egress (s3:GetObject, s3:CopyObject), credential creation (iam:CreateAccessKey, sts:GetSessionToken), and persistence (iam:AttachRolePolicy, lambda:CreateFunction with the assumed role); audit every other IAM role with a similar trust-

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
