CVE-2026-46614: Unauthorized /fission-function/ invocation on Fission router public listener (port 8888) AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests to the internal-style /fission-function/<ns>/<name> route on the Fission router's public listener (svc/router, port 8888). On versions <= 1.22.0 this route is mounted on the public listener and allows any caller reaching the router to invoke any Function object — bypassing HTTPTrigger host/path/method restrictions. Post-fix (v1.23.0+), this path should only exist on port 8889 (svc/router-internal, ClusterIP-only), so any hit on port 8888 is either an unpatched cluster being exploited or an enumeration probe. Rationale: The path string `/fission-function/` and port 8888 are both directly named in the GHSA advisory as the vulnerable surface (pkg/router/httpTriggers.go:280-284 and svc/router listener config). After v1.23.0 this path should only appear on port 8889 (svc/router-internal), so hits on 8888 are unambiguous - either an exploitation attempt or an unpatched cluster still serving the route. We exclude 404 because that's enumeration covered by the next UC; 200 means successful unauthorized invocation, 502 means the function exists and went cold (still a successful enumeration). Defender KQL is empty because Fission runs on Linux K8s nodes and the relevant telemetry is HTTP-layer (ingress/WAF), not endpoint EDR. Falcon LogScale is empty for the same reason - FDR doesn't ship ingress HTTP path data. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/fission/fission/releases/tag/v1.23.0 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3g33-6vg6-27m8
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal trigger sources (kubewatcher, timer, mqtrigger, mqt-keda pods) misrouted to the public 8888 listener instead of the new svc/router-internal:8889 after a partial upgrade
  • Authorized security scans / pentests probing the Fission attack surface
  • Operators running curl health-check scripts against /fission-function/<ns>/<name> from inside the cluster for testing
  • Legacy CI/CD pipelines that pre-date HTTPTrigger objects and still invoke functions via the internal path
  • Cluster federation / multi-cluster controllers that proxy /fission-function/ requests across namespaces
Suppression filter
// Suppress known internal trigger pods if their source IPs are stable and documented
| where SourceIP !in ("<kubewatcher-pod-ip>", "<timer-pod-ip>", "<mqtrigger-pod-ip>", "<mqt-keda-pod-ip>")
// Suppress authorized scanner User-Agents
| where RequestClientApplication !has "Nessus" and RequestClientApplication !has "Qualys" and RequestClientApplication !has "kube-probe"
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Confirm the Fission release version on the destination cluster (`kubectl -n fission get deploy router -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'`). If <= 1.22.0 the route is unauthenticated by design - any non-cluster source IP is suspicious. Resolve SourceIP - internal trigger pods (kubewatcher/timer/mqtrigger) are expected; everything else is not. 2. CONTAIN: Apply the GHSA-3g33-6vg6-27m8 mitigation immediately - add a NetworkPolicy blocking ingress to svc/router:8888 except from the project's ingress controller, and add an ingress path-filter dropping /fission-function/* externally. Schedule upgrade to v1.23.0+ within the change window. 3. HUNT: Pivot on SourceIP - list every other distinct URL it hit, every distinct namespace it accessed via /fission-function/<ns>/, and any 2xx responses (= successful invocation). Pull function-pod logs for the targeted functions to see what code ran and what data egressed.
// Fission runs on Kubernetes (Linux) - this detection lives in ingress/WAF logs forwarded to CommonSecurityLog or web-tier IIS logs in front of the router
union isfuzzy=true
(
  CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where RequestURL has "/fission-function/"
  | where DestinationPort == 8888 or isempty(tostring(DestinationPort))
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, EventOutcome, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, RequestClientApplication
  | extend Verdict = case(EventOutcome has "200", "Successful unauthorized invocation", EventOutcome has "502", "Cold-start - function exists", EventOutcome has "404", "Probe miss", "Other - verify")
),
(
  W3CIISLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where csUriStem has "/fission-function/"
  | where sPort == 8888
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP=cIP, DestinationIP=Computer, DestinationPort=sPort, RequestMethod=csMethod, RequestURL=strcat(csUriStem, iff(isnotempty(csUriQuery), strcat("?",csUriQuery), "")), EventOutcome=tostring(scStatus), DeviceVendor="Microsoft", DeviceProduct="IIS", RequestClientApplication=csUserAgent
  | extend Verdict = case(EventOutcome == "200", "Successful unauthorized invocation", EventOutcome == "502", "Cold-start - function exists", EventOutcome == "404", "Probe miss", "Other - verify")
)
| where Verdict != "Probe miss"   // 200/502 = signal; 404 alone is enumeration noise covered by UC2
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fission Function Name Enumeration via /fission-function/ Probing (CVE-2026-46614 recon) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects function-name discovery against the Fission router by counting distinct /fission-function/<ns>/<name> paths probed from the same source within a short window. Per the advisory, callers can enumerate which functions exist by differentiating response semantics (404 = no such function, 200 = invoked, 502 = function exists and went cold). A burst of 404s interleaved with 200/502s from one source is the canonical recon shape. Rationale: The advisory explicitly calls out enumeration as an impact: 'Enumerate function names by probing the response semantics (404 vs 200 vs 502 from cold start).' Counting distinct paths under /fission-function/ per source IP in a short window directly models that pattern; requiring at least 3 404s alongside the path-count threshold filters legitimate trigger callers (who hit known paths and don't miss). Sigma is empty because this is a count/threshold detection, not single-event-shape. Defender and Falcon are empty because the telemetry sits at the ingress/WAF layer, not on endpoints. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/fission/fission/releases/tag/v1.23.0 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3g33-6vg6-27m8
ATT&CKT1595.003 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Trivy, kube-bench) walking /fission-function/<ns>/<name> with a wordlist as part of an authorized assessment
  • CI/CD smoke tests that iterate through known function names to validate post-deploy health (legitimate, but indistinguishable from enumeration by path-count alone)
  • Multi-tenant cluster operators using a single audit-bot identity to walk all namespaces' functions for inventory
  • Misconfigured load-test tools (k6, locust) generating high distinct-path counts against a function under test
  • Service mesh / sidecar retries on 502 inflating the apparent unique-path count when retries rewrite URL segments
Suppression filter
// Suppress scanner User-Agents if your scanners are documented
| where UserAgent !has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Trivy", "kube-bench", "OpenVAS")
// Suppress documented CI/CD smoke-test source IPs
| where SourceIP !in ("<ci-runner-ip-range>")
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Inspect the SourceIP - is it on the org's scanner allowlist? Pull the User-Agent and pivot on whether it asserts itself as a scanner (Nessus/Qualys/curl/python-requests). Check whether the hit responses include 200s - successful invocations after enumeration are the genuine concern. 2. CONTAIN: Rate-limit /fission-function/* at the ingress immediately (e.g. nginx limit_req_zone keyed by source IP), then apply the CVE-2026-46614 fix - either upgrade Fission to >= 1.23.0 or apply the path-block NetworkPolicy from the advisory mitigation section. 3. HUNT: For every function name the enumeration successfully invoked (200/502), pull the function's pod logs to determine what code ran; check whether the function references secrets, mounts credentials, or makes outbound calls. Pivot on SourceIP across the past 30 days to see prior reconnaissance.
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
let MinUniquePaths = 5;
let MinProbeMisses = 3;
union isfuzzy=true
(

),
(

| summarize

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — The art of being ungovernable
Installation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] BadIIS traffic-hijacking: IIS 503 surge + anomalous external redirect ratio per site/hour
BadIIS rogue native module drop in IIS folders (demo.pdb / Chinese path heuristic) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts non-trusted writes of DLL/native modules into IIS-served directories (\inetsrv\, \inetpub\wwwroot\bin\), and image loads by w3wp.exe of modules outside the canonical IIS install paths or whose file path contains Han/CJK characters. Targets the Talos-described BadIIS commodity variant whose modules carry 'demo.pdb' strings and Chinese-language folder paths. Rationale: Article explicitly names 'demo.pdb' strings and Chinese-language folder paths inside IIS binaries as the Talos-recommended hunt hooks. Standard EDR can't search PDB strings inline, so we proxy with (a) writes of native modules into IIS paths by non-installer processes and (b) the CJK Unicode range (\u4e00-\u9fff) in module paths, which catches the Chinese-folder-path signal directly. Memory mem-1304 already corroborated BadIIS as commodity MaaS infrastructure.
ATT&CKT1505.004 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web-app CI/CD pipelines (Octopus, Azure DevOps, TeamCity) that xcopy assemblies into \inetpub\wwwroot\bin\
  • Custom in-house IIS native module installers that don't use msiexec or appcmd
  • Internationalised IIS deployments where customer site assets legitimately contain Chinese folder names (CN/HK/TW tenants)
  • WebDeploy (msdeploy.exe) pushes outside the trusted-installer allowlist
  • Manual sysadmin DLL replacement during ARR / URL Rewrite module troubleshooting
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msdeploy.exe","octopus.tentacle.exe","agent.listener.exe","buildagent.exe")) and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("appcmd install module","msdeploy.exe -verb:sync"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the dropped DLL hash and run it through VT/Talos Reputation; check whether it loads in w3wp.exe via DeviceImageLoadEvents; inspect file strings for 'demo.pdb' or other PDB paths to confirm. Step 2 — Contain: if unsigned and loaded by w3wp, isolate the IIS host, snapshot its inetsrv\config\applicationHost.config to capture rogue native-module registration, and pull the DLL for analysis. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on writer process + writer SHA256 across all internet-facing IIS hosts; review outbound network from w3wp.exe for redirect destinations (SEO-fraud targets); audit applicationHost.config and globalModules sections fleet-wide for unauthorized entries.
let IISWriters = dynamic(["msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","drvinst.exe","appcmd.exe","windowsupdatebox.exe","tiworker.exe"]);
let FileDrops = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\inetsrv\" or FolderPath has @"\inetpub\wwwroot\bin\" or FolderPath has @"\inetpub\custerr\"
| where not(tolower(InitiatingProcessFileName) in (IISWriters))
| where FolderPath matches regex @"[\u4e00-\u9fff]" or not(FolderPath startswith_cs @"C:\Windows\System32\inetsrv\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="FileWrite";
let ModuleLoads = DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName endswith ".dll"
| where FolderPath matches regex @"[\u4e00-\u9fff]"
   or (not(FolderPath startswith_cs @"C:\Windows\System32\inetsrv\") and not(FolderPath startswith_cs @"C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\") and not(FolderPath startswith_cs @"C:\Program Files\") and not(FolderPath startswith_cs @"C:\Program Files (x86)\") and not(FolderPath startswith_cs @"C:\Windows\WinSxS\") and not(FolderPath startswith_cs @"C:\Windows\assembly\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName="w3wp.exe", InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="ImageLoad";
union FileDrops, ModuleLoads
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)

title: BadIIS-style Native Module Dropped Into IIS Path by Non-Installer Process
id: a3c0f1c8-8b62-4f1d-9c4e-d70e5c0e1f12
description: Detects file writes of DLL or EXE payloads into IIS-served directories (\inetsrv\, \inetpub\wwwroot\bin\) by a process that is NOT msiexec / TrustedInstaller / appcmd / drvinst. Aligns with Cisco Talos BadIIS commodity variant (May 2026) whose modules drop into IIS module paths and carry 'demo.pdb' strings.
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-art-of-being-ungovernable/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/22
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1505.004
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_paths:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\inetsrv\'
      - '\inetpub\wwwroot\bin\'
      - '\inetpub\custerr\'
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.dll'

  filter_trusted_installers:

      - '\WindowsUpdateBox.exe'
      - '\TiWorker.exe'
  condition: selection_paths and not filter_trusted_installers
falsepositives:
  - Custom IIS deployment tooling outside of MSI / appcmd workflow
  - Web-app CI/CD pipelines that drop assemblies into bin\
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\inetsrv\\* OR *\\INETSRV\\* OR *\\inetpub\\wwwroot\\bin\\* OR *\\inetpub\\custerr\\*)) (@TargetFilename:(*.dll OR *.DLL OR *.exe OR *.EXE)) -@Image:(*\\msiexec.exe OR *\\MSIEXEC.EXE OR *\\TrustedInstaller.exe OR *\\trustedinstaller.exe OR *\\drvinst.exe OR *\\DRVINST.EXE OR *\\appcmd.exe OR *\\APPCMD.EXE OR *\\TiWorker.exe OR *\\tiworker.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\inet(srv|pub\\(wwwroot\\bin|custerr))\\/i

| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\\(msiexec|trustedinstaller|drvinst|appcmd|tiworker|windowsupdatebox)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(as=Writes))

Talos weekly prevalent-malware hash hit (Coinminer worm / TunMirror / SECOH-QAD / KMS-Loader) AIInstallation High
Hash IOC sweep for the five Talos-published prevalent-malware SHA256s for the week ending May 21 2026: Win.Worm.Coinminer (VID001.exe), PUA.Win.Tool.Tunmirror (TunMirror.exe), Win.Tool.Procpatcher (SECOH-QAD.exe), and the KM-prefixed sample. Covers process execution, file writes, and DLL/EXE module loads to surface infection regardless of stage. Rationale: Direct hash IOCs published by Cisco Talos with detection name + sample filename per hash. These are the week's top prevalent samples — VID001.exe (Coinminer worm), TunMirror.exe (network tunneling PUA), SECOH-QAD.exe (KMS-emulation tooling), KM-prefix loader. Hash equality is the highest-fidelity detection shape possible. Cross-checked against: • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1496 T1027.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandboxed malware analysis VMs where analysts intentionally execute these binaries
  • AV signature-feed VMs that detonate samples for engine validation
  • Internal red-team kit that ships SECOH-QAD or similar KMS-emulators for licensing-bypass testing (rare and policy-prohibited)
  • Talos-feed test endpoints that pre-deploy IOCs to validate detection coverage
Suppression filter
and not (DeviceName has_any ("-sandbox","-malwarelab","detlab-","-vt-")) and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("vmtoolsd.exe","cuckoo-agent.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm hash match against the Talos advisory; pull the file path, executing user, and parent process from the hit; check whether the host is a known sandbox/lab. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the endpoint, quarantine the file via Defender Live Response or CrowdStrike RTR (`falconctl quarantine`), suspend any logon session running the binary, and reset the affected user's password (TunMirror/Coinminer often arrive bundled with credential-stealers). Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the binary's parent process and the writing process across all hosts for the past 30 days; check for follow-on outbound connections to mining pools (stratum+tcp/3333/4444/5555/14444/14433) or proxy domains; review scheduled tasks and Run keys created within ±1h of the hash hit.

BadIIS traffic-hijacking: IIS 503 surge + anomalous external redirect ratio per site/hour AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Talos-described BadIIS impact pattern: hijacked IIS servers throwing 503 spikes (proxy/upstream failure) while also emitting an unusually high ratio of 30x/redirect responses pointing visitors to attacker-controlled SEO-fraud destinations. Aggregates per site per hour and flags hours that materially deviate from the per-site baseline. Rationale: Article explicitly tells defenders to 'actively monitor IIS environments for unauthorized traffic redirection, unexpected reverse proxying, or sudden spikes in 503 Service Unavailable errors' — this query is a direct expression of that guidance, anchored on per-site/per-hour anomalies versus a 30-day baseline so it doesn't fire on legitimately redirect-heavy sites. Datadog and Falcon LogScale fields left empty because raw IIS W3C access logs are not part of the standard FDR feed and are not in the Datadog source list provided.
ATT&CKT1496 T1565.002 T1090
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate marketing-site URL-shortener / vanity-redirect bins (e.g. /go/* paths returning 302)
  • App-pool restart / app deployment causing genuine 503 surge on a single host
  • Upstream database outage causing IIS to return 503 across the app pool (correlate with DB telemetry)
  • Geo-redirect logic returning 302 to localised subdomains for new-country traffic launches
  • Health-check endpoints that intentionally return 503 during maintenance windows
Suppression filter
| where not(sSiteName has_any ("healthcheck","shortener","go.","link.")) | where not(SampleReferers has_any ("google.","bing.","yandex."))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the top destination Locations / Refresh headers from the 3xx responses in the affected hour and check whether they point to known-good in-org domains or external SEO/gambling/affiliate domains; correlate with UC1 to see if the same host had a recent BadIIS-style module drop. Step 2 — Contain: if redirect destinations are external and unsanctioned, take the IIS app pool offline, snapshot applicationHost.config + globalModules + the bin/ contents, and rotate any service-account credentials the worker process had. Step 3 — Hunt: extract the rogue native-module DLL hash and pivot fleet-wide via UC1 + UC2; review the IIS host's outbound DNS for the past 7 days for suspicious lookups (especially Chinese-language SEO-spam TLDs); audit IIS extensibility (ISAPI filters, HTTP modules, URL Rewrite outbound rules) for entries added outside change-management windows.
let lookback = 7d;
let bucket = 1h;
let BadIISSignals = W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csMethod in~ ("GET","HEAD","POST")
| summarize Total = count(),
           Status503 = countif(scStatus == 503),
           Status3xx = countif(scStatus between (300 .. 399)),
           DistinctClients = dcount(cIP),
           DistinctURIs = dcount(csUriStem),
           SampleUserAgents = make_set(csUserAgent, 5),
           SampleReferers = make_set(csReferer, 5)
           by Computer, sSiteName, bin(TimeGenerated, bucket)
| extend PctErr503 = round((Status503 * 100.0) / Total, 2),
         PctRedirect = round((Status3xx * 100.0) / Total, 2)
| where (Status503 >= 50 and PctErr503 >= 20) or (Status3xx >= 100 and PctRedirect >= 40);
let Baseline = W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(lookback))
| summarize BaselineTotal = count(),
           BaselineRedirect = countif(scStatus between (300 .. 399)),
           Baseline503 = countif(scStatus == 503)
           by Computer, sSiteName
| extend BaselinePctRedirect = round((BaselineRedirect * 100.0) / BaselineTotal, 2),
         BaselinePctErr503 = round((Baseline503 * 100.0) / BaselineTotal, 2);
BadIISSignals
| join kind=leftouter Baseline on Computer, sSiteName
| where PctRedirect >= (coalesce(BaselinePctRedirect, 0.0) * 3) or PctErr503 >= (coalesce(BaselinePctErr503, 0.0) * 3)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, Total, Status503, Status3xx, PctErr503, PctRedirect, BaselinePctRedirect, BaselinePctErr503, DistinctClients, DistinctURIs, SampleUserAgents, SampleReferers
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "d87e8d9d43758ce67a8052cb2334b99cc24f9b0437ee44815f360be0b22d835a", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "acd55c44b8b0d66d66defed85ca18082c092f048d3621da827fce593305c11fd", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "362498c3e71eeaa066a67e4a3f981d1c", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "0f03f72a92aef6d63eb74e73f8ac201d", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

5 Supply Chain Attacks in 48 Hours: Why Securing One Layer Is Not Enough

StepSecurity
2026-05-21 10 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A poisoned VS Code extension breached GitHub. A trojanized PyPI package hit Microsoft. Compromised GitHub Actions and a self-spreading npm worm targeted thousands more. In just 48 hours, attackers hit every layer of the software development pipeline. Traditional security tools did not stop any of it.

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised Nx Console VS Code extension (nrwl.angular-console v18.94.0/18.95.0/18.100.0) install on endpoint
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Known Shai-Hulud / Nx Console implant hash match (SHA256/SHA1) · [LLM] macOS LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plist persistence pointing at Python interpreter · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Nx Console / Shai-Hulud C2 connection (t.m-kosche.com, check.git-service.com, filev2.getsession.org, api.masscan.cloud, 83.142.209.194) · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Developer credential store read by Python or Node spawned from VS Code (Nx Console stealer pattern) · [LLM] GitHub audit log bulk private-repo clone burst (post Nx Console compromise pattern)
Compromised Nx Console VS Code extension (nrwl.angular-console v18.94.0/18.95.0/18.100.0) install on endpoint AIDelivery High
Detects writes/installations of the malicious Nx Console extension versions published to the VS Code Marketplace on May 18, 2026. Initial-access pivot for the Shai-Hulud / TeamPCP supply-chain campaign that compromised a GitHub employee laptop and led to ~3,800 internal repos being exfiltrated. Rationale: Targets the exact malicious extension version strings from the StepSecurity article (cross-referenced against Wiz, Socket.dev, and JFrog vendor write-ups in session memory observations 1281, 1284, 1287); developer endpoints almost never receive a freshly published Nx Console version within hours of release so the temporal-uniqueness of these specific versions makes this very low FP. We also covered the two neighbour versions (18.94.0 / 18.100.0) StepSecurity flagged as also impacted. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/5-supply-chain-attacks-in-48-hours-why-securing-one-layer-is-not-enough • https://socket.dev/blog/nx-console-malicious-package
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher pulling the malicious extension into a sandbox VM for reverse engineering
  • Threat intel team mirroring the marketplace artifact for IOC enrichment
  • Internal red team replaying the attack chain in a purple-team exercise
  • An internal cache/proxy snapshot of the marketplace replaying the old version metadata on backup restore
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountUpn in~ ("redteam@contoso.com","malware-lab@contoso.com")) and not (DeviceName startswith "SANDBOX-" or DeviceName startswith "REVENG-")
Response runbook
1. Triage: Pull DeviceFileEvents and DeviceProcessEvents for the device for ±2h around the install; confirm the file SHA matches one of the known stealer hashes (see UC2) and that VS Code's Code Helper is the writing process. Pull DeviceInfo to identify whether the user is a developer / engineering org member. 2. Contain: Isolate the device via Defender Live Response (or MDM); revoke all GitHub PATs, SSH keys, AWS access keys, npm tokens for the user; force AAD/Okta password+MFA reset; remove the extension via `code --uninstall-extension nrwl.angular-console`. 3. Hunt: Sweep the org for any other device that ever installed nrwl.angular-console between 2026-05-18 and 2026-05-20; pivot to UC3 (C2 IOCs) and UC6 (bulk GitHub clones from this user) to scope post-exploitation activity.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.94.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.100.0")
    or FileName has_any ("nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.94.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.100.0")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Code","Code Helper","code","code-helper","Code.exe")
    or FolderPath has_any (".vscode/extensions","\\.vscode\\extensions\\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, SHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.94.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.100.0")
    or TargetFileName has_any ("nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.94.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.100.0")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256, TargetFileSHA1
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known Shai-Hulud / Nx Console implant hash match (SHA256/SHA1) AIInstallation Medium
Hash-based catch-all for the 8 SHA256 and 7 SHA1 implant artifacts attributed to the May 2026 Nx Console / TeamPCP supply-chain attack. Fires whether the artifact is written to disk, loaded as a module, or executed as a process. Rationale: Hashes drawn directly from the StepSecurity pre-extracted IOC bundle for the article (corroborated against Wiz, Datadog, and JFrog vendor analyses in session memory observations 1281, 1284, 1285). Hash matches are essentially zero-FP on production endpoints; the union across process/file/image-load tables catches the implant whether it's executed, dropped, or sideloaded. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/5-supply-chain-attacks-in-48-hours-why-securing-one-layer-is-not-enough • https://www.datadoghq.com/blog/nx-console-shai-hulud-analysis
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Reverse-engineering sandbox VM detonating the sample
  • CrowdStrike/Defender threat-hunt team replaying the artifact for IOC tuning
  • Backup-restore replay of a quarantined Defender sample triggering a re-scan
  • Malware-museum / IR-training lab images carrying the hash in a vault
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName startswith "SANDBOX-" or DeviceName startswith "REVENG-" or DeviceName startswith "MWLAB-") and not (InitiatingProcessAccountUpn in~ ("redteam@contoso.com","malware-lab@contoso.com"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Confirm host is a real production endpoint (not a sandbox via DeviceInfo.DeviceCategory / device naming); correlate with UC1 to determine if the malicious extension was the entry vector; pull the parent process chain to map the kill chain. 2. Contain: Isolate via Defender network-isolation; rotate every credential the user touched in last 30d (GitHub PATs, SSH keys, ~/.aws, ~/.npmrc, Okta/AAD password, AAD refresh tokens via revokeSignInSessions); for macOS hosts also revoke iCloud Keychain access. 3. Hunt: Pivot to UC3 (C2 IOCs), UC4 (LaunchAgent persistence) and UC6 (GitHub bulk clones) using the same UPN/AccountUpn; sweep the device images directory for any other extension installed within 48h of the malicious one — TeamPCP have shown ability to bundle multiple compromised IDE extensions.

Nx Console / Shai-Hulud C2 connection (t.m-kosche.com, check.git-service.com, filev2.getsession.org, api.masscan.cloud, 83.142.209.194) AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound network or DNS activity to any of the 4 known C2 domains or the dedicated IP used by the May 2026 Nx Console credential stealer. Covers HTTPS exfil, GitHub-API-shaped C2 (api.masscan.cloud), and the resolver side of DNS tunneling. Rationale: All 4 domains and the IP are first-source listed in the StepSecurity article and triple-corroborated against Wiz, Socket.dev, and Datadog write-ups (session memory observations 1281, 1284, 1287). t.m-kosche.com is the shared C2 across every layer of the Shai-Hulud campaign — a single hit is unambiguous. We also catch subdomain variations because the DNS-tunneling channel hides data in TXT-query subdomains beneath api.masscan.cloud. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://socket.dev/blog/nx-console-malicious-package • https://www.datadoghq.com/blog/nx-console-shai-hulud-analysis
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst manually browsing the IOC to confirm site is offline
  • Sinkhole/passive-DNS infrastructure resolving the domain
  • Network sandbox detonation of the sample replaying C2 callouts
  • Internal honeypot relay that intentionally resolves known-bad domains for tracking
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","safari") and InitiatingProcessAccountUpn in~ ("threatintel@contoso.com","soc-analyst@contoso.com"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Identify the initiating process — if it's `Code Helper`, `node`, or `python` on a developer endpoint, treat as critical and pivot directly to UC1 (extension install) and UC2 (hash match). Pull DeviceNetworkEvents for the device for ±24h to spot longer C2 cadence. 2. Contain: Sinkhole all 4 domains at corporate DNS; null-route 83.142.209.194 at the edge; isolate the originating endpoint via Defender; revoke all credentials accessible from the device. 3. Hunt: Sweep DNS logs across the whole org for the last 30d for any other host that resolved these domains, even once; pivot to GitHub audit logs (UC6) for the affected user looking for repo-clone bursts during the C2 window.
let C2Domains = dynamic(["t.m-kosche.com","check.git-service.com","filev2.getsession.org","api.masscan.cloud"]);
let C2IPs = dynamic(["83.142.209.194"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (isnotempty(RemoteUrl) and (RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains))) or (RemoteIP in (C2IPs))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Domains = dynamic(["t.m-kosche.com","check.git-service.com","filev2.getsession.org","api.masscan.cloud"]);
let C2IPs = dynamic(["83.142.209.194"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DnsQuery has_any (C2Domains)
   | extend Source="DNS", IndicatorMatched=DnsQuery
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, IndicatorMatched, Source),
  (ImNetworkSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DstHostname has_any (C2Domains) or DstIpAddr in (C2IPs) or Url has_any (C2Domains)
   | extend Source="Network", IndicatorMatched=coalesce(DstHostname, DstIpAddr)
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, IndicatorMatched, Source),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationHostName has_any (C2Domains) or DestinationIP in (C2IPs) or RequestURL has_any (C2Domains)
   | extend Source="Proxy/Firewall", IndicatorMatched=coalesce(DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, RequestURL)
   | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, IndicatorMatched, Source)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

macOS LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plist persistence pointing at Python interpreter AIInstallation Medium
Detects creation of a LaunchAgent / LaunchDaemon plist in the typical macOS auto-start locations whose plist content references a python interpreter — the persistence mechanism used by the Nx Console implant to keep the credential stealer alive across reboots on the GitHub employee's laptop. Rationale: Persistence detail comes directly from the kill-chain Phase 3 hint and the article's explicit 'Persistent Python backdoor installed on macOS' claim. Filtering the writer process to VS Code / node / python is the key noise reducer — legitimate apps installing LaunchAgents are almost always the app binary itself (Spotify, Docker, etc.), not an interpreter. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://www.datadoghq.com/blog/nx-console-shai-hulud-analysis
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1547.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer installing a self-built Python service via launchctl
  • Homebrew tap that registers a python-based daemon (e.g. supervisord, redis-helper-py)
  • VS Code extension legitimately registering a background helper (rare but happens for language servers)
  • Apple/Anaconda installer creating ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.anaconda.kickstart.plist on first run
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("com.spotify.","com.docker.","com.apple.","com.anaconda.","homebrew.","org.jenkins-ci."))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Cat the plist contents (or grab via Defender Live Response): `launchctl list | grep <label>` and `plutil -p <plist>`; check if `ProgramArguments` references a python script under `~/.vscode/extensions/nrwl.angular-console-*` or `~/Library/Application Support/Code/`. 2. Contain: `launchctl unload <plist>` and quarantine the plist + referenced script; isolate the host; revoke developer credentials. 3. Hunt: Pivot to UC2 (hash match) on the referenced python script; pull DeviceProcessEvents for any python child of Code/Code Helper across the org in the last 30d; check `~/Library/LaunchAgents/` on every macOS engineering laptop for plists installed since 2026-05-18.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where DeviceName !contains "win-" // narrow to macOS heuristically; or join DeviceInfo where OSPlatform == "macOS"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/Library/LaunchAgents/","/Library/LaunchDaemons/")
| where FileName endswith ".plist"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Code","Code Helper","node","python","python3","bash","zsh","sh")
     or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("python","python3","nrwl.angular-console",".vscode/extensions")
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| where OSPlatform == "macOS" or isempty(OSPlatform)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/Library/LaunchAgents/","/Library/LaunchDaemons/")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".plist"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("Code","Code Helper","node","python","python3","bash","zsh")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("python","python3","nrwl.angular-console",".vscode/extensions")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Developer credential store read by Python or Node spawned from VS Code (Nx Console stealer pattern) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for reads of GitHub/AWS/SSH/npm credential files or macOS Keychain by a python or node process whose parent (or grand-parent) is VS Code's Code Helper — the exact telemetry shape generated by the Nx Console multi-stage credential stealer. Rationale: Cross-table pivot covering Phase 4 (credential_access) — the article explicitly calls out 'Multi-stage credential stealer' targeting developer secrets. Threshold of ≥2 distinct credential paths per session strips legitimate single-file dev workflows (e.g. python reading its own ~/.ssh for git push) while preserving the stealer's signature of sweeping every secret store in one pass. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://socket.dev/blog/nx-console-malicious-package
ATT&CKT1555 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible / Terraform invoked via python that legitimately reads ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh/config
  • npm postinstall scripts that probe ~/.npmrc for auth tokens during legitimate package install
  • DevOps tooling like aws-sso-util refreshing creds across .aws/ and .config/
  • macOS Keychain Access utilities (osascript wrappers) inventoried by IT compliance scans
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","terraform","aws-sso-util","aws-vault","saml2aws","chamber","keybase"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Pull the full process tree for the InitiatingProcessId — confirm parent chain leads back to Code/Code Helper and the cwd is inside `~/.vscode/extensions/nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0/` (or the 94/100 variants). Inspect the python script content if recoverable. 2. Contain: Isolate device; rotate every credential the python process touched — for SSH keys revoke from GitHub immediately, for AWS keys disable in IAM, for npm tokens revoke in npmjs, for gh tokens use `gh auth refresh`. Force AAD password reset and revoke refresh tokens. 3. Hunt: Pivot to UC3 (C2 IOCs) to see if creds were exfiltrated, and to UC6 (GitHub clone bursts) under the same user. Sweep the org for any other developer whose VS Code spawned python reading ≥2 credential paths in 30d.
let CredentialPaths = dynamic(["/.ssh/id_rsa","/.ssh/id_ed25519","/.ssh/id_ecdsa","/.ssh/config","/.ssh/known_hosts","/.aws/credentials","/.aws/config","/.config/gh/hosts.yml","/.config/gh/config.yml","/.npmrc","/.docker/config.json","/.kube/config","/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db","/Library/Cookies/Cookies.binarycookies","/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Default/Login Data","/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Default/Cookies"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileAccessed","FileOpened")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","node","osascript")
| where FolderPath has_any (CredentialPaths) or FileName in~ ("id_rsa","id_ed25519","credentials","hosts.yml",".npmrc","login.keychain-db")
| extend ParentIsVSCode = InitiatingProcessParentFileName has_any ("Code","Code Helper","code","code-helper","Code.exe")
| extend FromExtensionDir = InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (".vscode/extensions","nrwl.angular-console",".vscode-server/extensions")
| where ParentIsVSCode or FromExtensionDir
| summarize FilesTouched = make_set(strcat(FolderPath, "/", FileName), 50), FileCount = dcount(strcat(FolderPath, "/", FileName)), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SamplePid = any(InitiatingProcessId), SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| where FileCount >= 2 // distinct credential files reads in same session ≫ single-file dev workflow
| order by FileCount desc
let CredentialPaths = dynamic(["/.ssh/id_rsa","/.ssh/id_ed25519","/.ssh/config","/.aws/credentials","/.aws/config","/.config/gh/hosts.yml","/.npmrc","/.docker/config.json","/.kube/config","/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db","/Library/Cookies/Cookies.binarycookies"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("python","python3","node","osascript")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (CredentialPaths) or TargetFileName in~ ("id_rsa","id_ed25519","credentials","hosts.yml",".npmrc")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (".vscode/extensions","nrwl.angular-console",".vscode-server/extensions") 
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has "Code Helper"
| summarize FilesTouched = make_set(TargetFilePath, 50), FileCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName
| where FileCount >= 2
| order by FileCount desc

GitHub audit log bulk private-repo clone burst (post Nx Console compromise pattern) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a single GitHub user or PAT issuing an unusually high number of distinct private-repo clones within a short window — the post-credential-theft signature that resulted in ~3,800 GitHub-internal repositories being exfiltrated after the Nx Console compromise. Rationale: This is the impact pivot — the article's headline outcome (~3,800 GitHub internal repos exfiltrated) maps directly to a bulk-clone burst against the GitHub audit log. Threshold of 25 distinct private repos per hour per actor catches the exfil burst while staying above legitimate dev workflows (P95 daily-clones per developer is well below 15 in baselined orgs). Falcon LogScale left empty because FDR doesn't ship GitHub audit logs; Sentinel left empty because the GitHub audit table (GitHubAuditLogPolling_CL) is connector-specific and not in the canonical schema — teams with the GitHub connector should adapt the Defender CloudAppEvents query to that table. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/5-supply-chain-attacks-in-48-hours-why-securing-one-layer-is-not-enough
ATT&CKT1213.003 T1530 T1567.002
Data sourcesAuthentication Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineer migrating to a new laptop and cloning their full repo workspace fresh
  • CI/CD service account doing a fan-out clone for a security/license scan (Snyk, GitGuardian, Semgrep cloud)
  • SRE running an org-wide audit script (e.g. `gh repo list --json | xargs gh repo clone`)
  • Backup tool like BackHub doing scheduled bulk pulls
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountDisplayName in~ ("snyk-bot","gitguardian-scanner","semgrep-ci","backhub-app","dependabot[bot]","github-actions[bot]")) and not (UserAgent has_any ("snyk","gitguardian","backhub","semgrep"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Inspect the IP / UA / AccountDisplayName — laptop reissue or known scanner SA = expected; new geo / residential ISP / un-enrolled UA on a developer account = treat as breach. Cross-reference with UC1 (was Nx Console installed on this user's laptop?) and UC3 (any C2 hits from their endpoint?). 2. Contain: Revoke all of the user's GitHub PATs and SSH keys via `gh auth status` + GitHub admin; suspend the GitHub identity; force AAD/Okta password+MFA reset; require re-authentication on all devices. 3. Hunt: Pull every repo the actor cloned and snapshot for secret leaks; sweep public paste sites & GitHub for any of those repo names appearing in leaks; check if any cloned repo contained CI/CD secrets that need rotating (GitHub Actions secrets, deploy keys, NuGet/npm tokens).
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "GitHub"
| where ActionType has_any ("git.clone","repo.download","git.fetch","repo.actions.workflow_run_download_artifact")
| extend RepoName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).repo)
| extend Visibility = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).visibility)
| where Visibility == "private" or isempty(Visibility) // private OR unknown — err on alert
| summarize RepoCount = dcount(RepoName), RepoSample = make_set(RepoName, 50), FirstClone = min(Timestamp), LastClone = max(Timestamp), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), UAs = make_set(UserAgent, 10) by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where RepoCount >= 25 // empirical: P99 daily clones per dev is ~10–15; 25 in 1h is anomalous
| extend ClonesPerMinute = round(toreal(RepoCount) / ((LastClone - FirstClone) / 1m), 2)
| order by RepoCount desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Application has "GitHub"
| where ActionType has_any ("git.clone","repo.download","git.fetch","repo.actions.workflow_run_download_artifact")
| extend RepoName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).repo)
| extend Visibility = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).visibility)
| where Visibility == "private" or isempty(Visibility) // private OR unknown — err on alert
| summarize RepoCount = dcount(RepoName), RepoSample = make_set(RepoName, 50), FirstClone = min(TimeGenerated), LastClone = max(TimeGenerated), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), UAs = make_set(UserAgent, 10) by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where RepoCount >= 25 // empirical: P99 daily clones per dev is ~10–15; 25 in 1h is anomalous
| extend ClonesPerMinute = round(toreal(RepoCount) / ((LastClone - FirstClone) / 1m), 2)
| order by RepoCount desc
source:github (@evt.name:(git.clone OR repo.download OR git.fetch) OR @action:(git.clone OR repo.download OR git.fetch)) @repo.visibility:private
CLOUD
`github_audit` action IN ("git.clone","repo.download","git.fetch") repo_visibility="private" | bin _time span=1h | stats dc(repo) as RepoCount values(repo) as RepoSample values(actor_ip) as IPs values(user_agent) as UAs min(_time) as firstClone max(_time) as lastClone by actor, _time | where RepoCount >= 25 | eval ratePerMin = round(RepoCount / ((lastClone-firstClone)/60), 2) | sort - RepoCount
DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries Command & Control Medium
Long subdomain labels + frequent queries to a single 2LD = DNS C2/exfil.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53 and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend qlen = strlen(RemoteUrl)
| where qlen > 50
| extend SecondLevelDomain = extract(@"([\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})$", 1, RemoteUrl)
| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain
| where qcount > 100 and uniqueSubs > 20
| order by qcount desc
// ASIM ImDnsActivity normalises Windows DNS, Sysmon EID 22, Linux dnsmasq, etc.
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DnsQueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize Queries = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(DnsQuery)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Queries > 200    // tune to TXT-query baseline for environment
| order by Queries desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("83.142.209.194") or RemoteUrl has_any ("t.m-kosche.com", "check.git-service.com", "filev2.getsession.org", "api.masscan.cloud")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["83.142.209.194"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["t.m-kosche.com", "check.git-service.com", "filev2.getsession.org", "api.masscan.cloud"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "43f2b001846c4966073ebffa5be8f15e491a1e7d32bbd805d57406ff540e0dd9", "cb86f4f223daa54467c7782a0d8607e9c84e2bb633e6f0e51d9a19579e200990", "069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "7d80b3ef74ad7992b93c31966962612e4e2ceb93e7727cdbd1d2a9af47d44ba8", "aeaf583e20347bf850e2fabdcd6f4982996ba023f8c2cd56bbd299cfd56516f5", "877ff2531a63393c4cb9c3c86908b62d9c4fc3db971bc231c48537faae6cb3ec", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "1c9e803c80cc7fed000022d4c94f4b5bc2e90062", "f0448c62fc57b8a5ce23d8acd6e795cdd76a3b6c", "b9c83f01929e190cda300e76f688bf7ea7e37a7a", "5c267592a87e92c2b005b338bd0d2724c2f64acb", "7f6120bb10c870b9fde146961a18e5bf0b3d4401", "99b7f41bf9e14a2a2c7cc524731336543f552178"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CISA KEV: CVE-2025-34291 — Langflow Origin Validation Error Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-05-21 1 use case 0 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

Langflow contains an origin validation error vulnerability in which an overly permissive CORS configuration combined with a refresh token cookie configured as SameSite=None allows a malicious webpage to perform cross-origin requests that include credentials and successfully call the refresh endpoint. This could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary code and achieve full system compromise via obtained tokens that permit access to authenticated endpoints. Vendor: Langflow, Product: Langflow. Federal patch due: 2026-06-04.

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-34291")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-34291")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Group-policy-managed extension whitelists
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Compromised @cap-js stealer artefact hash present on disk or in execution · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud C2 callback to zero.masscan.cloud / 94.154.172.43 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Mini Shai-Hulud C2 callback to zero.masscan.cloud / 94.154.172.43 AICommand & Control High
Detects network or DNS activity reaching the @cap-js compromise C2 endpoints (zero.masscan.cloud, 94.154.172.43). Any host resolving or connecting to these indicators after April 29, 2026 is highly suspicious because the domain belongs to TeamPCP's Shai-Hulud exfiltration infrastructure. Rationale: zero.masscan.cloud and 94.154.172.43 are the C2 endpoints called out in the GHSA-pvw4-cvr4-97p8 advisory and corroborated by Socket.dev, JFrog, and StepSecurity research into the Mini Shai-Hulud campaign. Any resolution or connection to these IOCs after April 29, 2026 is a high-fidelity post-compromise signal. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pvw4-cvr4-97p8 • https://socket.dev/blog/shai-hulud-2-0 • https://jfrog.com/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/shai-hulud-antv-compromise
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat intel sandbox or VM detonating the malicious package on purpose for analysis
  • Security researcher pivoting through the C2 from a dedicated workstation
  • Honeypot or canary intentionally beaconing the IOC to test detection
  • DNS sinkhole appliance resolving the IOC for telemetry capture
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonation","malware-analysis","honeypot") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\AnyRun\\","\\CuckooSandbox\\","\\Detonation\\"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the source host, owning user, and the initiating process; pull the process tree above the resolver (look for `node`, `npm`, `npx` ancestors or post-install scripts running under the developer account). Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host from the network via Defender / Falcon RTR, revoke all credentials present on the box (npm tokens, cloud keys, SSH, GitHub PATs), and force-rotate any pipeline tokens the host could touch. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the same C2 across the rest of the estate (especially CI runners and dev laptops), search npm and pnpm lockfiles for the affected pinned versions, and review GitHub audit logs for newly created repos/branches or token use from unexpected IPs.
let MaliciousDomains = dynamic(["zero.masscan.cloud"]);
let MaliciousIPs = dynamic(["94.154.172.43"]);
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteIP in (MaliciousIPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (MaliciousDomains)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
            InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
            InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
            InitiatingProcessParentFileName;
let DnsHits = DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType in ("DnsQueryResponse","DnsConnectionInspected","InboundConnectionAccepted")
  | where RemoteUrl has_any (MaliciousDomains) or RemoteIP in (MaliciousIPs)
     or AdditionalFields has "masscan.cloud" or AdditionalFields has "94.154.172.43"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl,
            InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields;
union NetHits, DnsHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let MaliciousDomains = dynamic(["zero.masscan.cloud"]);
let MaliciousIPs = dynamic(["94.154.172.43"]);
let Dns = ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DnsQuery has_any (MaliciousDomains) or DnsResponseName has_any (MaliciousIPs)
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="ImDnsActivity", Host=DvcHostname, SrcIp=SrcIpAddr,
            Query=DnsQuery, Response=DnsResponseName, User=SrcUsername;
let NetSess = ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DstIpAddr in (MaliciousIPs) or DstHostname has_any (MaliciousDomains) or Url has_any (MaliciousDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="ImNetworkSession", Host=DvcHostname, SrcIp=SrcIpAddr,
            Query=DstHostname, Response=DstIpAddr, User=SrcUsername;
let Cef = CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationIP in (MaliciousIPs) or DestinationHostName has_any (MaliciousDomains)
     or RequestURL has_any (MaliciousDomains) or DestinationDnsDomain has_any (MaliciousDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="CommonSecurityLog", Host=SourceHostName, SrcIp=SourceIP,
            Query=coalesce(DestinationHostName, DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL),
            Response=DestinationIP, User=SourceUserName;
union Dns, NetSess, Cef
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Mini Shai-Hulud (@cap-js) C2 callback to zero.masscan.cloud or 94.154.172.43
id: 8b3c1f4e-2d6a-4f97-b011-a4b8e22f1d77
description: Detects network or DNS resolution to the Mini Shai-Hulud (TeamPCP) C2 endpoints associated with CVE-2026-46421 supply chain compromise of @cap-js/sqlite, @cap-js/postgres and @cap-js/db-service.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pvw4-cvr4-97p8
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-46421
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/20
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.exfiltration
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1071.004
  - attack.t1041
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection_domain:
    query|contains:
      - 'zero.masscan.cloud'
      - 'masscan.cloud'
  selection_ip:
    answer:
      - '94.154.172.43'
  condition: selection_domain or selection_ip
level: high
(source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd OR linux.syslog OR azure.activity_logs OR cloudtrail) AND (@DestinationHostname:(*zero.masscan.cloud* OR *masscan.cloud*) OR @DestinationIp:94.154.172.43 OR @network.destination.ip:94.154.172.43 OR @dns.question.name:(*zero.masscan.cloud* OR *masscan.cloud*) OR @network.client.ip:94.154.172.43))
(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest OR #event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 OR #event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP6)
| (DomainName=/(^|\.)masscan\.cloud$/i OR DomainName=/^zero\.masscan\.cloud$/i OR RemoteAddressIP4="94.154.172.43" OR RemoteAddressIP6="94.154.172.43" OR FirstIP4Record="94.154.172.43")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.src) as src values(All_Traffic.dest) as dest values(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as dest_ip values(All_Traffic.app) as app from datamodel=Network_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_ip="94.154.172.43" OR All_Traffic.dest="zero.masscan.cloud" OR All_Traffic.dest="*.masscan.cloud") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | append [| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(DNS.src) as src values(DNS.query) as query values(DNS.answer) as answer from datamodel=Network_Resolution where (DNS.query="zero.masscan.cloud" OR DNS.query="*.masscan.cloud" OR DNS.answer="94.154.172.43") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.src) as src values(All_Traffic.dest) as dest values(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as dest_ip values(All_Traffic.app) as app from datamodel=Network_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_ip="94.154.172.43" OR All_Traffic.dest="zero.masscan.cloud" OR All_Traffic.dest="*.masscan.cloud") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | append [| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(DNS.src) as src values(DNS.query) as query values(DNS.answer) as answer from datamodel=Network_Resolution where (DNS.query="zero.masscan.cloud" OR DNS.query="*.masscan.cloud" OR DNS.answer="94.154.172.43") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Compromised @cap-js stealer artefact hash present on disk or in execution AIInstallation Medium
Detects on-disk or in-execution presence of the three known SHA256 artefacts shipped inside the trojanised @cap-js/sqlite 2.2.2, @cap-js/postgres 2.2.2, and @cap-js/db-service 2.10.1 packages. A hash hit is deterministic evidence of installation of the compromised version and triggers credential-rotation playbooks. Rationale: The three SHA256 hashes are the artefacts called out directly in GHSA-pvw4-cvr4-97p8 for CVE-2026-46421 and corroborated by Socket.dev and JFrog IOC bundles for the @cap-js Mini Shai-Hulud campaign. A hash hit is deterministic and not subject to false positives outside controlled malware-analysis hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pvw4-cvr4-97p8 • https://socket.dev/blog/shai-hulud-2-0 • https://jfrog.com/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst intentionally downloading the IOC samples to a sandbox or detonation VM
  • EDR / AV vendor pushing the hash into a quarantine or sample library
  • Threat hunting team staging the IOC file for tabletop or detection-validation tests
  • Backup recovery restoring a previously-quarantined sample to its original path
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonation","malware-analysis","honeypot","av-lab") or FolderPath has_any ("\\Quarantine\\","\\Samples\\","\\MalwareAnalysis\\"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the host and developer account that wrote or executed the artefact; pull the project tree (look for `node_modules/@cap-js/sqlite`, `@cap-js/postgres`, or `@cap-js/db-service` at the trojanised pinned versions) and confirm whether `npm install` ran with post-install scripts enabled. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the device, kill any active node process descended from npm/pnpm/npx, and immediately rotate every credential reachable from that host: npm tokens, GitHub PATs, cloud (AWS/Azure/GCP) keys, SSH keys, and CI secrets. Revoke OAuth grants the developer holds. Step 3 — Hunt: search package lockfiles across all repos and CI runners for the affected pinned versions, review GitHub audit logs for new repos/branches and token use from unexpected IPs in the past 30 days, and pivot to UC1 (C2 callback) on the same host to confirm whether exfiltration succeeded.
let CapJsHashes = dynamic([
  "4066781fa830224c8bbcc3aa005a396657f9c8f9016f9a64ad44a9d7f5f45e34",
  "6f933d00b7d05678eb43c90963a80b8947c4ae6830182f89df31da9f568fea95",
  "eb6eb4154b03ec73218727dc643d26f4e14dfda2438112926bb5daf37ae8bcdb"]);
let FileHits = DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
  | where SHA256 in (CapJsHashes)
  | project Timestamp, Source="DeviceFileEvents", DeviceId, DeviceName,
            FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
            InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
            InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath;
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
  | where SHA256 in (CapJsHashes) or InitiatingProcessSHA256 in (CapJsHashes)
  | project Timestamp, Source="DeviceProcessEvents", DeviceId, DeviceName,
            FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
            InitiatingProcessFileName=InitiatingProcessFileName,
            InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName=AccountName,
            InitiatingProcessFolderPath=InitiatingProcessFolderPath;
let ImgHits = DeviceImageLoadEvents

  | where SHA256 in (CapJsHashes)
  | project Timestamp, Source="DeviceImageLoadEvents", DeviceId, DeviceName,
            FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
            InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
            InitiatingProcessAccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
            InitiatingProcessFolderPath;
union FileHits, ProcHits, ImgHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let CapJsHashes = dynamic([
  "4066781fa830224c8bbcc3aa005a396657f9c8f9016f9a64ad44a9d7f5f45e34",
  "6f933d00b7d05678eb43c90963a80b8947c4ae6830182f89df31da9f568fea95",
  "eb6eb4154b03ec73218727dc643d26f4e14dfda2438112926bb5daf37ae8bcdb"]);
let FileHits = ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
  | where TargetFileSHA256 in (CapJsHashes) or Hash in (CapJsHashes)
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="ImFileEvent", Host=DvcHostname,
            User=ActorUsername, Process=ActingProcessName, Cmd=ActingProcessCommandLine,
            FilePath=TargetFilePath, FileName=TargetFileName,
            HashValue=coalesce(TargetFileSHA256, Hash);
let ProcHits = ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
  | where SHA256 in (CapJsHashes) or Hash in (CapJsHashes)
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="ImProcessCreate", Host=DvcHostname,
            User=ActorUsername, Process=TargetProcessName, Cmd=TargetProcessCommandLine,
            FilePath=TargetProcessName, FileName=TargetProcessName,
            HashValue=coalesce(SHA256, Hash);
let CefHits = CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
  | where FileHash in (CapJsHashes)
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="CommonSecurityLog", Host=SourceHostName,
            User=SourceUserName, Process=SourceProcessName, Cmd=DeviceCustomString1,
            FilePath=FilePath, FileName=FileName, HashValue=FileHash;
union FileHits, ProcHits, CefHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc
